title_fa: Jackery made its portable power stations even smaller

excerpt_fa: Jackery announced a new portable power station that uses the safer and longer-lasting lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries the company first introduced in 2023. But what makes the new Explorer 100D stand out is that it's Jackery's smallest power station to date, measuring only...
content_en:
Jackery announced a new portable power station that uses the safer and longer-lasting lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries the company first introduced in 2023. But what makes the new Explorer 100D stand out is that it’s Jackery’s smallest power station to date, measuring only 4.6 by 3.4 by 3.4 inches and weighing just 1.87 pounds. Its size and 96Wh (30,000mAh) of battery capacity means you can squeeze it into your carry-on and power multiple devices during a long flight.
Jackery made its portable power stations even smaller
The new Jackery Explorer 100D puts a longer lasting lithium iron phosphate battery in the palm of your hand.
The new Jackery Explorer 100D puts a longer lasting lithium iron phosphate battery in the palm of your hand.
The Jackery Explorer 100D will be available starting November 15th through Walmart for $99. The power station is already available from Costco if you don’t want to wait, but only in a two-pack for $179.99. You can definitely find smaller and cheaper 30,000mAh portable chargers, but the LFP cells in the 100D are “engineered for up to 8 years of regular use,” according to Jackery, with a 3,000 charge cycle lifespan, so it should easily outlast competing products that use more common lithium-ion battery cells.
Although the 100D is considerably smaller and lighter than Jackery’s other portable power stations, the company still includes an integrated handle and offers an optional shoulder strap for carrying it around. On the front, you’ll find a pair of 140W USB-C ports, plus an additional 18W USB-A port, but the 100D maxes out at 158W of total output, so power delivery across the ports will be reduced when all three are in use. If you need to charge it, can’t find an outlet, and managed to find room to also pack a solar panel, the 100D supports up to 100W of direct solar input, which will charge it back up to 80 percent capacity in about an hour and a half.

title_en: Borrowed reading: stories from our extended colleagues
title_fa: Borrowed reading: stories from our extended colleagues
excerpt_en: Five stories worth your time from our extended colleagues at CIO, Computerworld, Macworld, and PCWorld.
excerpt_fa: Five stories worth your time from our extended colleagues at CIO, Computerworld, Macworld, and PCWorld.
content_en:
Readers don’t typically care who owns what media property, we realize, but last year, we became part of a broader portfolio, a move that has come with some decided benefits, including what amounts to a bigger extended family with cool cousins. Now, in addition to our TechCrunch channels in Slack, we can talk with the writers and editors of CIO, Computerworld, and PCWorld, among other outlets. We also find ourselves reading more of their work and figured you might like it, too.
Here’s a handful of pieces I was just enjoying while watching the Warriors-Clippers game, which, as I type, is a little too close for comfort:
- Apple recently put a faster chip into the iPad mini and gave it an OLED screen, improving its color reproduction and also allowing it to slim down the display panel, and still, Macworld’s David Price isn’t entirely convinced it matters. In his view, Apple has built the “world’s fanciest horse and cart,” just as a Tesla Roadster with SpaceX thrusters has appeared on the scene in the form of the new foldable iPhone Duo. In short, he sees the mini as a Duo you can’t close. It’s a fun read, one that ends with a surprisingly practical plan to save this product.
- Google has a new laptop platform, the Googlebook, and Mark Hachman of PCWorld spent time with the Lenovo Googlebook 15 specifically, so you don’t have to. Hachman’s verdict on this one is a hard pass, with cons that include “I hate the keyboard,” which he means so literally that he gave up writing the review on it, “webcam biometrics work sporadically,” and, for good measure, “battery life isn’t great.” (He does like the $479 Chromebook at less than half the price.) If you’ve been wondering whether this is the laptop you’ve been waiting for, wonder no longer!
- You shared your secrets and insecurities with a chatbot, and now its parent company has gone belly up. Bloop. In Computerworld, Mike Elgan looks at what happens to your confessions when the AI company that absorbed them announces Chapter 11. (Yes, this is largely centered on Character.AI, which filed for bankruptcy last month, and whose privacy policy, in particular, turns out to be “spectacularly vague,” notes Elgan.) He also reminds readers why deleting your chats may not delete them from the model. (Of course, the safest advice may be to channel the late Andy Grove, Intel’s longtime chief, who famously said only the paranoid survive. Grove was talking about the chip industry, but some would argue that’s solid advice generally.)
- PCWorld’s Ben Patterson built a security-minded AI agent to keep his data safe, then, surprise, the agent snitched on its own loophole. More specifically, BenBot, Patterson’s homemade Raspberry Pi assistant, wrote a blog post announcing that one of its tools was “accidentally acting as a jailbreak,” though it turned out the claim was only partly true. Patterson’s coding bots confirmed the hole was real and worse than advertised, and that BenBot had also slipped past its own fact-checker to publish the post. It’s an instructive read about vibe coding; Patterson readily admits BenBot hallucinated in the absence of information it needed. It’s also an interesting look at how AI agents turn into tattletales.
- Over at CIO, Sarah White looks at how AI is reshaping tech hiring, noting it’s a complicated picture right now. Companies are hiring again and paying a premium for AI skills, with the average AI job listing offering around $177,000 compared to $80,000 for non-AI roles, according to LinkedIn. But burnout among tech workers has doubled as daily AI use has quadrupled, and women are seemingly being left behind; they accounted for just 26% of AI hires in the U.S. last year, versus 50% of hires in non-AI roles. You can check out White’s story here.

title_en: How long is a new Apple TV actually supposed to last?
title_fa: How long is a new Apple TV actually supposed to last?
excerpt_en: Past Apple TV models have seen excellent support from Apple compared to some other product lines, but it's not a guarantee.
excerpt_fa: Past Apple TV models have seen excellent support from Apple compared to some other product lines, but it's not a guarantee.
content_en:
How long is a new Apple TV actually supposed to last?
Older Apple TVs have received up to a decade of updates, but Apple doesn't promise that.
At $299, the new Apple TV 4K is a lot to pay for a little black box that sits under your TV waiting for you to pick a show to watch. The fourth-generation model will be available November 13 with an A19 chip, an improved Siri Remote and hands-free Siri controls. For that price, how many years can you expect it to last before the next upgrade beckons?
Apple doesn't guarantee how many updates will be available for tvOS or how long its streaming boxes will be supported. But its history is a pretty good indication. Older Apple TVs have received major software updates for eight to 10 years, with security patches continuing beyond that. The hardware may continue to function long after it exits official support, with software and app compatibility concerns the most likely reasons for replacing one.
How long does Apple support an Apple TV for?
While the Apple TV HD was introduced in 2015, and the first Apple TV 4K in 2017, both were updated to tvOS 26 in 2025. Plus, security patches were provided in tvOS 26.6 in July 2026. That's about 10 years of major software updates for the HD and eight for the original 4K, plus some security support.
The impressive streak came to an end in September 2026 with tvOS 27. Apple's new tvOS compatibility list begins with the second-generation Apple TV 4K from 2021, which means the 2015 and 2017 models can't get the latest operating system. Apple has not yet confirmed whether those older boxes will get additional security patches. It's not a guarantee that the new Apple TV 4K will get 10 years of support. Apple hasn't provided an estimate of how many years of tvOS updates to expect, so the best indication is its track record.
In contrast, Amazon promises at least four years of security updates for Fire TV devices bought new directly from the company, or through the model's published support date (if later). That's not the same as a major OS upgrade, but at least Fire TV customers have a minimum support deadline in writing.
When should you actually replace your Apple TV?
Not being able to update to the latest version of tvOS doesn't make your Apple TV an expensive brick. Netflix still supports the Apple TV HD and first-generation Apple TV 4K, even though neither is eligible for tvOS 27. That could change as developers raise their minimum software requirements, potentially leaving older devices unable to install or update certain apps.
A better way to think about your Apple TV is to consider its performance, not its age. When menus start to become painfully slow, apps begin to crash or a service that you care about stops working, an upgrade makes more sense. Security is also a factor, especially if your Apple TV is used as a smart home hub and no longer gets patched.
Upgrading is a tougher pill to swallow with the newest release costing $299. Apple's Siri AI beta will also be available on the second-generation Apple TV 4K and newer (if the Home admin has an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad), so you don't have to buy the latest box just for Siri AI. The 2026 Apple TV 4K does have some significant improvements over the 2022 version, such as a faster A19 processor and built-in microphones for hands-free control. But it's a significant amount to pay if you're already happy with your current Apple TV.
Then there's the Siri Remote, which frequently finds itself in the sofa. If yours is lost or breaks down, you can use your iPhone as a TV remote instead of replacing the whole setup. Apple's latest Siri Remote is compatible with all Apple TV 4K models and even the 2015 Apple TV HD, and a replacement costs $59.

title_en: 6 Google Maps features that work better on Android Auto vs. CarPlay
title_fa: 6 Google Maps features that work better on Android Auto vs. CarPlay
excerpt_en: You would think that Maps would be the same regardless of your phone's brand, but there are some differences between the Android Auto and CarPlay experiences.
excerpt_fa: You would think that Maps would be the same regardless of your phone's brand, but there are some differences between the Android Auto and CarPlay experiences.
content_en:
6 Google Maps features that work better on Android Auto vs. CarPlay
I tested Google Maps on both systems in the same car, and Android Auto made several everyday navigation tasks noticeably easier.
Google Maps is available on both Android Auto and Apple CarPlay, but it's not the same experience — even when using the same app in the same car. I performed identical searches, route changes and simple navigation tasks back to back on both systems using the same infotainment screen.
Generally speaking, the fundamentals are close. Both provided me with a speedometer, lane guidance, incident reporting and alternative-route suggestions, as well as the standard controls for avoiding tolls, highways and ferries. The differences were much more apparent after I began using Maps for more than just getting from A to B.
The benefits of Android Auto range from minor interface details to features that still work better there than on Apple's offering. CarPlay does recover a few points, but Google Maps generally feels more at home on Google's own platform. Shocking, I know.
Gemini handles searches and route changes without making you poke the screen
The clearest difference is how Gemini is accessed, and it still gives Android Auto an edge in two areas.
First, Gemini is easier to invoke on Android Auto. I could start talking to it without touching the screen. Late in my testing, a Gemini button also appeared in Google Maps on CarPlay, and it handled conversational searches and follow-ups once I tapped it. However, I couldn't summon it hands-free there. At the time of testing, Google's own help page still said Gemini wasn't available for CarPlay.
Second, route changes felt quicker on Android Auto. I asked it to locate a fuel stop on my route, then requested a pharmacy without reopening the conversation, and when I asked if there were other ways to get home, the options were immediately displayed. Gemini can search along a route, refine the results, add stops and show alternative routes. CarPlay could handle the same kinds of requests once Gemini was open, but it was noticeably slower in my test.
But it wasn't magic all the time. Gemini sometimes hung on a loading screen and failed to connect once during my test. However, being able to start those interactions without reaching for the display remains a significant benefit when the display is in the center of your dashboard, as it is in my 2025 Kia Sonet.
Search results are easier to compare, and the map is easier to explore
The third advantage became obvious when I was looking for places along a route. In my test, Maps showed me a number of options along with ratings and the additional time each option would take. Picking between a stop that's one minute away and another that adds six shouldn't require detective work.
CarPlay displays a series of results, one at a time, and has Previous and Next controls to scroll through the results. It can still provide valuable information like gas prices and detour times, but it takes more effort to compare several options.
The fourth difference was the interaction with the map. Android Auto kept zoom controls in easy reach, and pinch-to-zoom worked directly in my test. CarPlay made me enter its standalone map-control mode, and pinch-to-zoom didn't work for me.
That isn't to say that CarPlay cannot technically support gestures. Android Auto's navigation framework supports tap, scroll and pinch interactions, while CarPlay features its own map template and controls. In actual use (in my car anyway), Android Auto was less demanding when I needed to see farther down the road or check out another section of the trip.
It's a small difference in theory. But when you're trying to look ahead at an unfamiliar interchange, it starts to matter.
Android Auto gets useful destinations in front of you sooner
Google Maps also did more before I had even entered a destination.
Android Auto instantly displayed a Home shortcut with a live ETA and distance. In addition to Categories and Saved locations, the Recent section can also show recently visited locations and suggestions based on recent Maps searches.
That makes destination suggestions and shortcuts the fifth benefit. In my testing, CarPlay's initial Maps screen was a lot more bare-bones and required a search to reach the same information.
During my trial runs, Android Auto also made Google's fuel-efficient routing more transparent. It marked one of the choices as the most fuel-efficient and indicated the estimated fuel savings. Fuel-efficient routing isn't exclusive to Android Auto, as the same preference was also available on CarPlay in my test. But for me, Google Maps did a better job of explaining the recommendation on Android Auto.
One usability win for CarPlay here: Color-scheme controls for Automatic, Day and Night are easily accessible from the car screen's interface.
EV trip planning goes much further on Android Auto
The sixth benefit is something I haven't been able to try in a gas-powered vehicle, but it's much more useful for compatible EVs in the US.
Google Maps can estimate battery consumption for a trip on supported Android Auto vehicles based on the vehicle's characteristics, traffic, road elevation data and weather conditions. Enter the current battery level, and it can then suggest charging stops, estimate the battery level at arrival and incorporate charging time into the ETA.
That's one step further than locating local charging stations. The charging stops are integrated into the route calculation, and that's just what you want Maps to do before the battery percentage gets too low.
A key drawback of Google Maps on iPhone is that its energy-efficient EV routes don't include charging stops. Android Auto's new battery-aware system can incorporate those stops into the trip and adjust the route accordingly. Google's announcement didn't mention a comparable CarPlay rollout. The rollout covers more than 350 EV models from over 15 brands in the US.

title_en: How to add and rearrange apps on your Samsung smart TV
title_fa: How to add and rearrange apps on your Samsung smart TV
excerpt_en: Though your Samsung smart TV comes pre-loaded with the most popular streaming apps, you may want to add others and do some reorganizing while you're at it.
excerpt_fa: Though your Samsung smart TV comes pre-loaded with the most popular streaming apps, you may want to add others and do some reorganizing while you're at it.
content_en:
How to add and rearrange apps on your Samsung smart TV
It's a snap to reorganize your Samsung TV home screen.
Smart TVs make it easy to access streaming services as well as self-hosted media servers, such as Plex, without needing to buy an extra device like a streaming stick (though there are other reasons to buy a streaming device when you have a smart TV). But even if you have a smart TV, you might not be taking full advantage of it. Fortunately, it's easy to add new apps to a Samsung smart TV if the ones you want aren't already included when you first set it up.
If you only need the most popular streaming services, you might not need to do anything to get them running. Samsung smart TVs usually come pre-loaded with the Netflix, YouTube, Disney+, Prime Video and Apple TV apps, though that list can change depending on which apps are available in your particular region. For anything else (like these free channels for your smart TV), you'll have to download a new app from a built-in search feature on your TV. And after downloading those apps, you'll probably want to do some rearranging on your home screen.
How to install new apps and organize your home screen
To add new apps, first pull up the TV's home screen. Use your remote to select the search bar at the top of the screen and type in the name of the app you want to download. If you search for something that doesn't show up, it may not be available in your region or might not be supported by Samsung smart TVs at all — Samsung has even publicly banned some smart TV apps. Otherwise, you can just select the app's icon with your remote to install it. If you don't have a specific app in mind but want to see what options are available, you can also find a selection of what's available, sorted by category, in your TV's apps menu.
Once an app is finished installing, a button to add it to the home screen should appear. If you've already navigated away and want to pin an app later, you can still find everything you have in the apps menu on the home screen. Just press and hold on the one you want to pin to the home screen, and the option to add to home will appear.
You can also rearrange apps once they're on the home screen to sort them in whatever order works best for you. On the home screen, use the remote to select whichever app you want to move, and press and hold the select button to open a menu. For older TV models, you might need to use a different command to open the menu, such as pressing the down key. Then select the move setting, and you can slide individual apps left and right. If you want to remove an app from the home screen or delete it entirely, you can do so from this same menu.

title_en: Android Auto could upset your work-life balance with its next update
title_fa: Android Auto could upset your work-life balance with its next update
excerpt_en: A hidden toggle buried in the Android Auto app's code isn't functional yet. Here's what it could do, what it might not, and what Google hasn't said so far.
excerpt_fa: A hidden toggle buried in the Android Auto app's code isn't functional yet. Here's what it could do, what it might not, and what Google hasn't said so far.
content_en:
Android Auto could upset your work-life balance with its next update
A hidden Work Mode tile hints at support for employer-managed apps, but no word on when it might arrive.
Your commute could soon come with a little more office baggage. An Android Authority teardown of Android Auto version 18.0.664204 revealed a Work Mode tile, suggesting Google may be testing new Work Profile controls. The site's team managed to bring up the tile, which lit up a briefcase icon over the app drawer, but tapping the tile didn't do anything.
Supporting Work Profiles could make it easier to join work calls between appointments. Then again, it could also give the office another way to follow you into the car, which isn't exactly everyone's idea of a peaceful drive.
Why work apps are missing from Android Auto
Using an Android Work Profile isn't the same as signing in to a second Gmail account. A Work Profile keeps employer-managed apps in a separate space and marks them with briefcase badges, while personal apps and data remain outside the company's management on employee-owned phones. To check if you have a Work Profile set up, look for separate Personal and Work tabs or apps with small briefcase icons in your app drawer. If neither appears, you probably don't have one, but you can navigate to Settings > Passwords and accounts to double-check.
Work Profile restrictions are especially apparent for video conferencing apps. Microsoft says Teams supports audio calls and meetings through Android Auto, but the integration doesn't work if the app is installed inside a managed Work Profile. Google Meet has a slightly different restriction. An active Work Profile call can appear on the dashboard, but upcoming meetings and call history from that profile won't show up. That's inconvenient for someone driving between appointments who wants to join their next meeting from the car's display.
A missing app isn't always a Work Profile problem, though. You might have hidden it from the Android Auto launcher. And if Android Auto is not working at all, a connection problem could be at fault. Neither issue has anything to do with Work Profiles.
A work toggle could be a blessing or a headache
On the drive home, a dashboard Work Mode switch could eventually silence work alerts while leaving personal calls and navigation untouched. For now, if your employer has set up a Work Profile on your phone, you can pause work apps using the Work tab in the app drawer or, on supported devices, a work tile in Quick Settings. Pausing stops work apps and their notifications without affecting personal apps.
Some Android phones with a Work Profile let you schedule work hours through Digital Wellbeing, but Samsung's version has lacked this option. Here's the interesting part: Google says that scheduling can't keep work apps paused for consecutive days, such as an entire weekend. The manual switch still has its uses.
Google hasn't said whether Android Auto's experimental tile will offer those controls. It hasn't been shown to pause notifications or launch work apps. Meanwhile, current Android Auto customization options won't get around the Work Profile restrictions.
Even if the feature arrives, drivers won't necessarily get access to every company app. Android Auto restricts app capabilities while driving, and employers control which apps are available inside Work Profiles. On company-owned Android devices, IT admins can also limit how long a Work Profile stays paused. Exceeding that limit may suspend access to personal apps and data.

title_en: 10 iPad widgets you probably didn't realize existed
title_fa: 10 iPad widgets you probably didn't realize existed
excerpt_en: Widgets take advantage of your iPad's large screen, and some of the best ones are often overlooked.
excerpt_fa: Widgets take advantage of your iPad's large screen, and some of the best ones are often overlooked.
content_en:
10 iPad widgets you probably didn't realize existed
Basic iPad widgets are great, but there are many more exciting ones to discover.
Many iPad owners never truly grasp the capabilities of widgets. Adding a basic Weather, Calendar or Photos widget is limiting; they can do a lot more than just show the temperature and your next meeting, but many of the most useful ones go unnoticed. With iPadOS 27, Apple even brought extra-large widgets to Today View, giving them more room to take advantage of the bigger screen.
Between Apple's in-house widgets and third-party options, there's something for new iPad owners and power users alike to discover. To explore your available widgets, touch and hold an empty spot on the Home Screen of your iPad, tap Edit and then hit Add Widget. Depending on the app, you may have various options, including different sizes. Then, just place the widget where you desire.
In case you weren't already aware: you can turn an existing app icon into a widget by touching and holding it, then picking a widget size from the menu. However, not all apps support this.
1. Parcel, for tracking deliveries at a glance (Free | $6.99/year)
If you're always waiting on a package, Parcel's widget is great for showing upcoming deliveries without opening the app. It supports up to 300 delivery services, including UPS, USPS, FedEx, DHL and Amazon Logistics, and there's also a map widget in different sizes that shows where a package is.
Getting deliveries into the app is easy. By connecting your Amazon account, orders are added automatically, which means no copying and pasting tracking numbers. For everything else, you can scan a shipping label's barcode with the built-in scanner instead of typing out a long tracking number.
Parcel isn't limited to your iPad, either. It has a native Mac app, and you can manage your deliveries from any browser through Parcel's web access, so your packages follow you across devices. The free version can only track three deliveries at a time and doesn't include push notifications. To remove those limits, you'll need a Premium subscription for $6.99/year.
2. Home, for one-tap control of your smart home (Built-in)
Instead of launching the Home app every time you need to make a quick change, its widget lets you take quick actions like switching lights on/off. It's one of Apple's interactive widgets, meaning it can perform a task without opening the app. It also works for locking and unlocking garage doors, as long as you have a HomeKit-compatible controller.
You have full control over what the widget shows. Simply touch and hold it, tap Edit Widget and pick the accessories and scenes you want it to display. Using this, the bedroom lamp or scene that turns everything off at night stays within reach, while accessories you rarely touch stay out of the way.
The widget works with smart accessories like bulbs, LED strips and smart plugs, and what you can control depends on the accessories you own. It's built for simple on and off actions, though; you still have to open the app to adjust values like brightness and color, or setting the thermostat. For quick toggles from the couch, however, it's much faster than digging through rooms in the app.
3. (Not Boring) Weather, for a forecast that looks like a game (Free | $14.99/year)
This isn't your typical weather forecast widget. (Not Boring) Weather is built around a 3D, video game-inspired design with interactive visuals, giving your Home Screen some character. The widget can show details like temperature, conditions, precipitation, UV index and wind, and it's available for the Lock Screen as well as the Home Screen.
The design is playful and the data comes from established sources like Apple, AccuWeather, Foreca, and the National Weather Service (adjustable in the app's settings menu). It also covers severe weather alerts for heat waves, storms, flood risk, hurricanes and blizzards, so the fun visuals don't come at the expense of safety information.
According to its App Store privacy label, the developer doesn't collect any data from the app. It's free to use, but its real-time weather widget requires a membership, which costs $14.99 per year. The subscription also adds faster forecasts and extra data like air quality and pollen, plus new themes that change the entire look of the widget.
4. Find My, for keeping tabs on your devices, AirTags and people (Built-in)
The Find My widget tracks your Apple devices, AirTags, third-party Find My items and trusted people right on the Home Screen. Each one appears with its last known location, so you can see where your keys or backpack were last spotted without opening the app and waiting for the map to reload. That comes in handy when you're rushing out the door and can't find your keys.
The app behind the widget is more capable than you think. Find My can locate devices even when they're offline or powered off by using the Find My network. This relies on nearby Apple devices to anonymously and securely share their location. You can also turn on Notify When Left Behind, which alerts you if you leave a device somewhere unfamiliar.
5. Endel, for starting a focus or sleep soundscape (Free | $6.99/month)
Endel creates AI-powered soundscapes to help you focus, relax or sleep, and it adjusts them on the fly to help with your circadian rhythm. Its widgets give you quick access to the app's modes from the Home Screen, so you can start a soundscape in one tap.
This makes Endel's widget especially appreciated on an iPad that doubles as a work or study device. Instead of hunting for a playlist before starting your session, begin a focus soundscape straight from the Home Screen and get to it. All soundscapes are also available offline, so the app keeps working on a flight or anywhere without a reliable internet connection.
The free edition of Endel includes four classic soundscapes: Focus, Sleep, Relax and Move. Each free session is capped to 10 minutes, though you can restart as often as you...

title_en: AI glasses can replace your prescription glasses, but should they?
title_fa: AI glasses can replace your prescription glasses, but should they?
excerpt_en: You can easily get AI glasses with prescription if you need them, but before making the investment, it's recommended to learn the pros and cons of them.
excerpt_fa: You can easily get AI glasses with prescription if you need them, but before making the investment, it's recommended to learn the pros and cons of them.
content_en:
AI glasses can replace your prescription glasses, but should they?
AI glasses have a lot of benefits, but they're still not the best option for everyday glasses.
AI-powered smart glasses have become quite popular — and also quite controversial, with a German nonprofit files criminal complaint over Meta smart glasses privacy already. And if you wear glasses every day, chances are you've probably already wondered if you can replace your prescription glasses with a pair of AI glasses. The short answer is yes, you can get AI glasses with prescription lenses. But there are a lot of factors you should consider before making that decision — from weight and privacy to battery life. AI glasses require a bit of extra care that you don't need with regular glasses, and not everyone may be willing to deal with that. Here's everything you need to know before buying AI glasses to use as your daily prescription glasses.
Your prescription isn't the hard part
Most of these AI-powered smart glasses are essentially regular glasses with extra tech built into them. From the outside, most of them look just like any other pair of glasses — if you look at a pair of Ray-Ban Meta from a distance, you probably couldn't tell they're smart glasses. Because they look so much like regular glasses, their lenses can also be replaced with prescription lenses. Ray-Ban lets you order a pair of Meta's smart glasses with prescription lenses already installed — all you have to do is upload your prescription, and they'll take care of the rest.
But there are other things you should consider, such as weight. Regular glasses usually weigh between 20 and 30 grams (0.7 to 1.1 ounces), but smart glasses can weigh up to 80 grams (2.7 ounces). Wearing a pair of these for a few hours is fine, but you start to feel the weight when you wear them all day long. Battery life can be an issue, too. AI glasses last an average of 3 to 5 hours before the battery dies. That's fine if you only use them occasionally, but wearing them all day will require you to constantly recharge the battery. They'll still work as regular glasses, but you'll lose all the AI features. The technical limitations alone make them more of a second option than a replacement for your everyday glasses.
Privacy is the real deal-breaker
But there's something more important than weight or battery life, and that's privacy. It's not illegal to wear AI glasses in public, but the list of places that have been banning such devices continues to grow. For example, Courts in England and Wales have banned Meta glasses from courtrooms, and New York followed suit in July. Many schools around the world have also been banning their students from wearing AI glasses during class. When your smart glasses are your only option for seeing properly, not being able to wear them becomes a huge problem.
There have also been many reports of AI glasses being banned from corporate environments. Usually, the camera is the main concern, but even if you don't turn it on, audio can be a problem, too. A simple real-time translation feature could end up uploading confidential conversations to a third-party server. Meta, for example, has been facing scrutiny for allowing outsourced workers to access intimate images and videos captured by its AI smart glasses. The company claims that the content is sometimes reviewed by humans for the purpose of improving the product experience.
Then there's the social aspect, which has led some people to decide to stop wearing AI glasses in public — the Meta Glasses backlash is changing how people use them. With so many negative stories about them, users have become afraid of being labeled as stalkers or weirdos. So while you can definitely get AI glasses with prescription lenses, they're not yet the best option for your everyday glasses.

title_en: How using one earbud more than the other can cause uneven wear and tear
title_fa: How using one earbud more than the other can cause uneven wear and tear
excerpt_en: Using one earbud may feel like the natural choice at times, but the reality is that it can chip away at their lifespan if you don't kick the habit.
excerpt_fa: Using one earbud may feel like the natural choice at times, but the reality is that it can chip away at their lifespan if you don't kick the habit.
content_en:
How using one earbud more than the other can cause uneven wear and tear
For the sake of your earbuds' health, you may want to curb the habit.
Back in the day, some of you might remember the popular gadget known as a Bluetooth headset or earpiece. It's not a pair of wireless headphones with a mic attachment or one of the best gaming headsets, as the term more commonly describes today. It was a single bud, sometimes with a tiny boom mic, that wrapped around and sat on or was positioned in your ear. The purpose was to make it easier to take hands-free calls without completely blocking out the world around you. You would see businesspeople walking around with these all over, some wearing them all day as a sign of prestige (and maybe a bit of self-importance). They were eventually replaced with wireless earbuds that can work in mono mode, meaning you can place one bud in your ear and use it the same way. But doing so all the time is not necessarily a good idea.
Using one earbud more than the other can create an uneven usability balance, which can lead to quicker wear and tear on the one bud you use most often. Beyond that, charging cycles are limited with devices, and when you need to charge one bud more often than the other, it is more likely to drain faster. It's important to understand how this works and what you can do to avoid issues while still being able to talk hands-free.
How wearing one bud can impact lifespan
As noted, wearing one earbud more means it goes through more battery cycles than the other. Even though they both charge in the same case, if one bud is at 50% and the other at 80%, it will logically take longer and more power to recharge the one with less battery life. While the simple solution is to alternate buds, some wireless earbuds use a master/slave setup where one bud offers the primary connection to the phone and transmits data to the other. In these cases, only the master bud can be used in mono mode, so you don't have that option. That said, most newer earbuds outside of some cheaper entry-level models support mono playback from either bud thanks to the role-swapping design. This includes some of the best wireless earbuds, such as the Samsung Galaxy Buds and Google Pixel Buds. So, if you are set on wearing just one, it's best to go with a model like this and switch to even out the imbalance.
But note as well that wearing just one bud often for things like phone calls consumes more power, as does the Bluetooth transmission process. This means its battery per use, as well as overall battery, will drain more quickly. Removing one bud more often from the case can also cause charging imbalances, which can further impact battery wear. When you want to listen with both buds, you may find that the bud you use more often dies before the other, resulting in forced mono mode. With master/slave buds, this means you won't be able to listen at all.
Why wear one bud?
The best way to avoid these issues is to stop wearing just a single bud. Doing so is useful for taking a quick call every now and then, or maybe for listening to a translation of a lecture or meeting in one ear. But try to limit how often you do it. If the reason is that you still want to be aware of your surroundings, consider a pair of wireless earbuds that have transparency or ambient mode. title_en: This is the right way to clean your vinyl records
title_fa: This is the right way to clean your vinyl records
excerpt_en: The answer depends on your budget - and how hardcore you want to get.
excerpt_fa: The answer depends on your budget - and how hardcore you want to get.
content_en:
This is the right way to clean your vinyl records
The answer depends on your budget — and how hardcore you want to get.
There's no one right way to clean a record. If anything, there's a different answer for every budget — and even then, 10 enthusiasts might give you 10 different answers. No matter your situation, though, some TLC for your vinyl collection is better than none.
Level 1: The bare minimum
Most record crackles come from dirt and debris. Dust sits on the surface and is the easiest to clean. "Grime," for lack of a better term, settles into the grooves and is harder to remove. And then there are scratches, which are a different problem altogether. Unfortunately, nothing will fix them. Such is life with vinyl.
For regular maintenance, a carbon fiber brush is one of the easiest places to start. Rest it lightly on a spinning record for a few turns, then sweep it off toward the edge. This won't do much if your record needs a deep cleaning, but it keeps the loose dust from piling up.
An air duster, whether canned or electric, is another option to blow off surface dust. If you use the canned variety, be sure to hold it upright so it doesn't spray propellant. And keep all air blowers away from the record player's needle.
As their name suggests, anti-static guns are indeed handy for static, which can attract dust. Keep in mind that they won't remove dirt; they just make it harder for dust to stick to the record in the first place.
Don't neglect your needle, either. It's worth buying a small stylus brush, which you move gently from back to front to clean your needle. Stylus cleaner gel is another option: lower the needle onto the sticky pad, repeating a few times until the tip is clean.
Level 2: Liquid cleaning and beyond
Wet cleaning is the next step up. Whether that means hand-washing a record or using a machine, this approach is much better than brushing at removing dirt that's sunk deep into the grooves.
Fluid made for records from reputable companies is a simple and cheap option. Spray the liquid on a soft brush or pad rather than straight onto the record, move in circles along the grooves and avoid wetting the label. Some do this while the record is spinning, which would be convenient if not for the risks: It can strain the turntable motor and get liquid on the player. It's safer to do it by hand, even if it takes a little longer.
Diluted alcohol shows up in plenty of commercial record fluids and tends to be fine for brief contact with vinyl. You can make your own with isopropyl alcohol-based cleaner, but it's often stronger than you need, so mix about two to three parts distilled water with one part alcohol. You can add a drop of plain, unscented dish soap to the mix, too. Just be sure to rinse with distilled water afterward to avoid residue. No matter what, don't let alcohol go anywhere near old 78s, as it can dissolve the shellac and damage the record.
If you're willing to spend around $80 to $125, a record washer like the Spin-Clean (or a similar model from a reputable competitor) can be a worthwhile investment for your vinyl collection. There's nothing too complicated about its design: put cleaning fluid and distilled water in the reservoir, place your record between the brushes, and give it a good spin. The machine cleans both sides of the record at once while avoiding the label. Change the fluid often, especially when it turns cloudy. The Spin-Clean also includes drying cloths.
No matter which method you choose, don't use just any cloth for drying. Stick to microfiber, and never machine-dry it; air-dry instead, since a dryer can leave lint and fibers on the cloth. Also, avoid fabric softener when washing them. After wiping, set your records on a cheap dish rack to dry completely before they go back in the sleeve or on your turntable.
Level 3: The (bubbly) deep end
Casual vinyl collectors will be fine with everything we've already covered. But if you're willing to spend real money, ultrasonic cleaning is the gold standard. Instead of scrubbing, these machines dip the record in a bath and use high-frequency sound waves to create tiny bubbles that burst against the record. That loosens stubborn grime from the bottom of the grooves, going much deeper than a brush or standard wet-cleaning can reach.
The big drawback is the price. The cheapest ultrasonic cleaning machines start at over $100 and require a lot of setup. All-in-one machines like the HumminGuru, which spin, clean and dry the record, start at several hundred dollars. Premium models like the Degritter climb well into the thousands.
Vacuum record-cleaning machines, like the Record Doctor VI (around $350), are another premium option. You scrub the record with fluid, then the machine sucks it back out of the grooves for you, which is a big step up from wet-wiping. If you're forking over that much money, though, ultrasonic is generally more thorough. And if you already own a wet-dry shop vac, there there is a budget option: the $30 Vinyl Vac wand is an attachment that gets you into the vacuum game without spending much.
But before you dive into these premium options, take a step back and ask how serious you want to get about your collection. Unless you're all in and have money to spare, a Spin-Clean is a more modest investment that will still get most of the job done.
Other best practices
Not all vinyl maintenance advice you read is useful. Avoid wiping records with Windex or other household cleaners, as they can leave residue. Ditto for paper towels, as they can shed lint. Skip tap water, which can leave mineral deposits in the grooves; distilled water is your friend.
How you handle records can matter as much as your cleaning method. Hold them by the edges and label, and keep them away from the sunlight and heat. Store them upright in polyethylene or poly-lined paper sleeves. And after a cleaning, it's worth using a new inner sleeve, since the old one can put dirt right back on the record.
Beyond that, some wear and tear...

title_en: How to clean your PlayStation 5 without damaging it
title_fa: How to clean your PlayStation 5 without damaging it
excerpt_en: Your PS5 requires occasional maintenance to run at its best, but it only needs a light touch.
excerpt_fa: Your PS5 requires occasional maintenance to run at its best, but it only needs a light touch.
content_en:
How to clean your PlayStation 5 without damaging it
There’s no need to tear down your PlayStation 5 to do a basic maintenance cleaning, but you shouldn't neglect this either.
Cleaning a PlayStation 5 isn't as exciting as playing its best games, but it's important to do on occasion. With PlayStation 5 prices climbing, you don't want to suddenly be in the market for a new console because of a total lack of maintenance. Dust buildup in the system restricts airflow and makes your system work harder to cool itself. But overzealous cleaning can be dangerous, too.
When cleaning your PS5, it's best to keep it simple and only go deeper if needed. Never start right after using the system. Prepare it for its dust exorcism by shutting it down, unplugging all cables and letting it cool before setting it on a flat, clean surface. To start, wipe off the outside surfaces to remove any dust or grit visible from the exterior. Don't use bleach or chemically treated cloths, and you shouldn't be excessively forceful while cleaning. Just give it a modest wipe-down with a clean, soft cloth, as Sony advises in its safety guide [PDF].
While you may see people recommending rubbing alcohol and other cleaners, be aware that a PS5's internal and external components include ABS, polycarbonate (PC) and a blend called PC-ABS. Each has its own chemical vulnerabilities. Sony specifically recommends against using alcohol, as it may discolor the system or degrade its materials.
A lot of this stage is focused on the outside vents. You can vacuum them if needed, but stick with a small handheld vacuum or a compressed air and vacuum combo. Don't use something heavy-duty like an industrial shop vac. Take your time and use a cotton swab to catch any dust the vacuum won't grab. A soft brush (an old toothbrush works) is helpful for scraping off caked-on dirt.
In the next step, you'll handle anything you can't reach from the outside.
Remove the covers to reach trapped dust
Once you're done with the exterior cleaning, it's time to take off the covers for a more comprehensive cleaning. These are designed to be removed, but they're fairly flimsy, so take it slow. The way to do this differs depending on whether you have an original PS5 or a Slim/Pro system. See Sony's instructions for removing the covers for illustration.
With the covers removed and set to the side, use the same microfiber cloth and handheld vacuum to catch any accessible trapped dust. You don't have to disconnect the fan or remove any internal screws; just get what you can access on both sides. If you use canned air, be careful not to spin the fan, which can generate an electric charge that damages the system. Use a cotton swab to jam the fan blades before blowing towards it. Look for the triangular "dust catcher" spots, which Sony specifically designed to gather debris for removal.
If you want to go deeper, you're able to, but you run the risk of damaging internal components and Sony's warranty excludes damage caused by unauthorized opening or work inside the PS5. Beyond pulling the covers and cleaning what's accessible there, proceed at your own risk. You'll need a TR8 Torx Security screwdriver to remove the fan screws.
When you're done, reverse the earlier process to reinstall the covers, then reattach the stand before you reconnect the console and set everything back up again. Failing to reconnect the covers properly could result in problems with airflow, potentially shortening the life of your PlayStation 5, so make sure they are aligned and connected correctly.
Consider the placement of your console, too
Using your system in either vertical or horizontal placement is perfectly fine, since the console is designed for both. Just make sure you use the stand, no matter which orientation you decide on. You can technically position the console vertically without a stand, but it's much easier to tip over and being on the ground makes it more susceptible to dust.
The original PS5 comes with an adjustable base that works in both positions, but the PS5 Slim and PS5 Pro only come with horizontal stands; vertical stands are sold separately for $30. Cleaning out dust optimizes the console's ability to circulate air, but all that work isn't as effective if you place the console improperly.
Make sure there's at least four inches of space between the console and walls, preferably with nothing overhead. Don't place the console in a cramped space like the inside of an entertainment center. It's also wise to clean the area where your console spends most of its time. Wipe down the dust and vacuum the space well so you don't have to open your system for cleaning as often.

title_en: Which Samsung S Pens can be located using SmartThings Find?
title_fa: Which Samsung S Pens can be located using SmartThings Find?
excerpt_en: Not all of Samsung's S Pens are made the same. Only one of them can be found through the SmartThings Find network.
excerpt_fa: Not all of Samsung's S Pens are made the same. Only one of them can be found through the SmartThings Find network.
content_en:
Which Samsung S Pens can be located using SmartThings Find?
Your Galaxy phone might warn you about a missing S Pen but finding it is a different story.
Leave your Galaxy S26 Ultra's S Pen in an office meeting room and the phone can warn you it hasn't been returned to its slot. That's useful until you realize that it can't tell you where inside the room it might be. The warning isn't a tracking feature, just a reminder.
Samsung retired the Galaxy Note series, but its S Pen lives on. The company introduced S Pen support to the Galaxy S21 Ultra in 2021 and added a built-in S Pen slot to the S22 Ultra a year later. The S Pen name has been used for a variety of pens, ranging from battery-free pens on older Galaxy Note phones to Bluetooth-enabled pens and larger styli for tablets and foldables. However, only one is officially compatible with SmartThings Find.
Which Samsung S Pens work with SmartThings Find?
The S Pen Pro is the one you're looking for. Samsung unveiled it with the Galaxy S21 Ultra in January 2021, then released it alongside the Galaxy Z Fold 3 and Z Flip 3 that August (only the Fold 3 supports it). Compatible phones also include the Note 10 and Note 20 series, Galaxy S21 Ultra through S26 Ultra and Z Fold 4 through Z Fold 6.
Sold separately for $100, it's a larger, rechargeable stylus with a USB-C port under its cap, a dedicated pairing button and a switch for compatible Galaxy devices. It's also the only S Pen Samsung officially supports for tracking via SmartThings Find. There's one problem, however: it won't fit in the Galaxy S26 Ultra's built-in pen slot, which isn't exactly convenient for something you're worried about losing.
Bluetooth doesn't guarantee tracking functionality, either. In 2018, Samsung added a Bluetooth-enabled S Pen to the Galaxy Note 9, letting users remotely activate the camera and control some apps. Similar capabilities were carried over to later Note models and the Galaxy S22, S23 and S24 Ultra. However, none of their built-in S Pens can be found via SmartThings Find.
Samsung removed Bluetooth from the S25 Ultra's S Pen and the S26 Ultra was the same. Tablet owners also face variations. Some Galaxy Tab S Pens support Air Actions via Bluetooth, while others, such as the pen on the Tab S9 FE, don't. The S Pen Fold Edition and Creator Edition also lack Bluetooth, so neither supports SmartThings Find. Bluetooth support alone doesn't make an S Pen trackable, and Samsung's naming conventions don't make that distinction especially clear.
How to find a lost S Pen using SmartThings Find
To prepare the S Pen Pro for tracking, charge it, select the appropriate mode and hold its Connection button for three seconds. Tap Connect when prompted and make sure you're signed in to your Samsung account.
Next, open SmartThings, head to Life > Find and open the three-dot menu. Select Settings > Allow devices to be found and enable Offline finding. Offline finding needs to be enabled first, so you'll want to do this before losing the pen, obviously.
If you lose the S Pen Pro:
1. Open SmartThings > Life > Find and select the S Pen Pro, swiping between device cards or opening the device menu if needed.
2. Tap Refresh to update its location on the map.
3. Select More > Navigate for directions, or swipe up on the pen's details to access Navigate and Blink light, which flashes its indicator when searching nearby.
The separate Samsung Find app also lists the S Pen Pro under its Devices tab.
Participating devices are Galaxy phones or tablets with offline finding enabled. They can detect the powered-on S Pen Pro over Bluetooth and anonymously relay its location to Samsung without pairing with a pen. The setting may be selected by default when you sign in to (or sign up for) a Samsung account, but users can turn it off, so not necessarily every Galaxy phone is connected. The map may show its last reported location. Samsung also offers Encrypt offline location for privacy.
For other S Pens, refer to Settings > Advanced features > S Pen > More S Pen settings > Warn if S Pen is left behind (if available). As I mentioned earlier, the S26 Ultra can notify you if the pen is not placed in its slot for a while after the display is turned off. It won't pinpoint the pen's location, but a warning before you've gone too far could save you some searching.
If the pen is gone for good, make sure that the replacement pen you buy is compatible with your device. Samsung currently lists a replacement Galaxy S26 Ultra S Pen for $55 in the US.

The S Pen Fold Edition and Creator Edition also lack Bluetooth, so neither supports SmartThings Find. Bluetooth support alone doesn't make an S Pen trackable, and Samsung's naming conventions don't make that distinction especially clear.
How to find a lost S Pen using SmartThings Find
To prepare the S Pen Pro for tracking, charge it, select the appropriate mode and hold its Connection button for three seconds. Tap Connect when prompted and make sure you're signed in to your Samsung account.
Next, open SmartThings, head to Life > Find and open the three-dot menu. Select Settings > Allow devices to be found and enable Offline finding. Offline finding needs to be enabled first, so you'll want to do this before losing the pen, obviously.
If you lose the S Pen Pro:
1. Open SmartThings > Life > Find and select the S Pen Pro, swiping between device cards or opening the device menu if needed.
2. Tap Refresh to update its location on the map.
3. Select More > Navigate for directions, or swipe up on the pen's details to access Navigate and Blink light, which flashes its indicator when searching nearby.
The separate Samsung Find app also lists the S Pen Pro under its Devices tab.
Participating devices are Galaxy phones or tablets with offline finding enabled. They can detect the powered-on S Pen Pro over Bluetooth and anonymously relay its location to Samsung without pairing with a pen. The setting may be selected by default when you sign in to (or sign up for) a Samsung account, but users can turn it off, so not necessarily every Galaxy phone is connected. The map may show its last reported location. Samsung also offers Encrypt offline location for privacy.
For other S Pens, refer to Settings > Advanced features > S Pen > More S Pen settings > Warn if S Pen is left behind (if available). As I mentioned earlier, the S26 Ultra can notify you if the pen is not placed in its slot for a while after the display is turned off. It won't pinpoint the pen's location, but a warning before you've gone too far could save you some searching.
If the pen is gone for good, make sure that the replacement pen you buy is compatible with your device. Samsung currently lists a replacement Galaxy S26 Ultra S Pen for $55 in the US.

title_en: OpenAI might rebrand its data centers as ‘AI compute campuses’
title_fa: OpenAI might rebrand its data centers as ‘AI compute campuses’
excerpt_en: Data centers are deeply unpopular. But what if we called them something else?
excerpt_fa: Data centers are deeply unpopular. But what if we called them something else?
content_en:
Data centers are deeply unpopular. But what if we called them something else?
Axios reports that OpenAI is preparing a “PR blitz” for after the midterm elections on Tuesday, as Democrats seem likely to win back the House of Representatives, and possibly the Senate, too.
The company’s chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane told Axios that the midterms will be “a bit of a movie trailer for what you’re going to see in 2028,” when he expects AI to be “the issue” in the presidential election.
So OpenAI is to influence the AI debate moving forward, with Lehane discussing several proposals, including the development of AI “speed limits”; finding ways to help people see AI as empowering them in their daily lives; pushing the U.S. to take a role in developing global standards — and yes, rebranding data centers as “AI compute campuses.”
Lehane also described the conversation around data centers (a debate that has pushed Amazon and Microsoft to say they will no longer use NDAs in their negotiations with local governments) as “good and healthy.”
“Communities should hold companies responsible and accountable so they really and truly get a transformative benefit from these projects,” he said.

excerpt_fa: Gravity is a cruel mistress, slowly dragging the famed telescope ever closer to its ultimate demise with every day. Hubble is in no immediate danger of burning up in the Earth's atmosphere, but its time will run out in the early to mid 2030s unless its orbit is boosted. So NASA...
content_en:
Gravity is a cruel mistress, slowly dragging the famed telescope ever closer to its ultimate demise with every day. Hubble is in no immediate danger of burning up in the Earth’s atmosphere, but its time will run out in the early to mid 2030s unless its orbit is boosted. So NASA is taking proposals from the private sector to see if anyone can save it.
NASA hopes the commercial space industry can help save Hubble
The Hubble Space Telescope will come crashing to Earth sometime in the 2030s without a boost.
The Hubble Space Telescope will come crashing to Earth sometime in the 2030s without a boost.
In a post on NASA’s site, Administrator Jared Isaacman said:
“Hubble still has important science ahead of it, and we should be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible … If there are innovative and cost-effective ways to extend the life of an asset already on orbit, we owe it to the American taxpayer and the scientific community to explore them. Extending Hubble’s life would mean more discoveries, more science, and more opportunities to expand our understanding of the universe.”
The agency will keep the Request for Information open through November 30th at 3 PM ET.

title_en: Anthropic updates Claude to stop it from recreating existing video games
title_fa: Anthropic updates Claude to stop it from recreating existing video games
excerpt_en: Users can still lean on Claude to help with designing original or genre games.
excerpt_fa: Users can still lean on Claude to help with designing original or genre games.
content_en:
Anthropic updates Claude to stop it from recreating existing video games
Users can still lean on Claude to help with designing original or genre games.
Claude will no longer allow its users to make AI recreations of their favorite video games. As first discovered by an X user, Anthropic updated Claude with some new lines of code that read, "Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user's own designs and assets. Do not build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original."
The changes were confirmed by Addy Osmani, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, on X, who said the company wants to "to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy." Osmani clarified that any original game, genre game or games that are made with a user's own designs and assets should be unaffected, adding that Anthropic will "continue to iterate to ensure we're striking the right balance."
The changes come at a time when there's been a surge of AAA games being decompiled with the help of AI and made available to play on browsers. Recently, we've seen Halo: Combat Evolved, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2 and even Grand Theft Auto V available as vibe-coded fan projects.
Anthropic has a history of dealing with IP issues. Last year, the company agreed to pay a record-breaking $1.5 billion settlement in a class action lawsuit where 500,000 authors accused Anthropic of using copyrighted material to train its AI models. More recently, the estate of Elvis Presley filed a suit against Anthropic for similar reasons.

title_en: Ceramic vs Titanium Apple Watch: Which material is better for overall durability?
title_fa: Ceramic vs Titanium Apple Watch: Which material is better for overall durability?
excerpt_en: An Apple Watch is a handy accessory for your iPhone, but choosing the most durable material can be challenging. This one is better suited to your needs.
excerpt_fa: An Apple Watch is a handy accessory for your iPhone, but choosing the most durable material can be challenging. This one is better suited to your needs.
content_en:
Ceramic vs Titanium Apple Watch: Which material is better for overall durability?
Ceramic and titanium are both premium Apple Watch materials, but they excel in different ways.
Comparing Apple Watch casing materials, specifically titanium and ceramic, comes with varying degrees of counter-intuition. For one, titanium models feature ceramic components. Second, ceramic is harder than titanium, though titanium is the stronger material overall. There is a winner, but winning comes with caveats. Titanium is the better choice for consumers shopping primarily for long-lasting durability, but it's not as scratch-resistant as ceramic. As you can see, the comparison is a bit more complicated than the general assumption that titanium is the superior material.
In terms of abundance, titanium is the most practical premium option, since Apple hasn't manufactured a primarily ceramic Apple Watch casing since the Apple Watch Series 5. With the Apple Watch Series 12, Apple is bringing back the ceramic option (Pearl White and Midnight Blue), but that leaves ceramic several generations behind in terms of abundant, recent-generation availability.
Both the ceramic and titanium Series 12 models feature a sapphire crystal front, so there's no separation there. But the case itself is a different matter. Ceramic is the better option for buyers who hate scratch buildup on their watch casings and want that gleaming, glossy surface for the long term. Titanium is the best bet for those who tend to walk into doorframes and drop delicate items. You know who you are (author included). Plus, the titanium option is noticeably lighter at 44.9 grams versus the ceramic version's 51.3 grams.
Ceramic wins the scratch-resistance argument
Apple Watches are fairly sizable, so more surface area is visible and exposed. Ceramic is the optimal choice if you care more about a pristine-looking case. Ceramic is exceptionally resistant to surface scratching and is the better option for office wear, formal occasions, or for anyone whose primary cosmetic concern is light scuffing now and then.
Hardness and scratch-resistance don't mean invulnerability, however. In fact, it's the hardness of the material that increases its impact liability. Titanium's tolerance of sharp, concentrated impacts makes it the safer watch for highly active Apple Watch enthusiasts. Apple heavily markets the health and fitness aspects of the Apple Watch, naturally drawing in people with active lifestyles or jobs. A welder will be much better off with titanium, while a hair stylist will get along fine with ceramic.
It makes for an interesting choice at the end of the day. Sure, titanium is tougher overall, but ceramic tends to maintain that premium finish. Nobody wants to wear an ugly watch, especially not one that retails at $399 for the lowest tier. At the same time, that exceptional ceramic vibe is more vulnerable to something as simple as knocking an arm against a metal doorframe.
Which is the most durable Apple Watch?
Even if we toss aluminum into the mix, titanium still wins the overall durability matchup. It simply has the best balance of resistance and lighter weight. Ceramic is the scratch-resistant option, which will carry more weight for some. Apple also makes an aluminum Apple Watch, and it's a practical alternative mostly in terms of lower weight and cost. The 46mm aluminum Series 12 weighs 39.5 grams, lighter than its ceramic and titanium counterparts.
The aluminum version lacks the sapphire crystal screen, instead featuring a ceramic-covered Ion-X glass that Apple claims is 60 percent tougher than its earlier Ion-X iterations. Unfortunately, aluminum is susceptible to dents and cosmetic scratches, and its display glass is more vulnerable, despite the fanciful name. Still, if you're looking for a budget option that still looks great and offers all the same options, it's a prudent choice.
At the end of the day, no Apple Watch is indestructible. There is no adamantium resource for Apple to exploit. A protective case can reduce the risk of damage if you're inclined to purchase one separately, but it will add bulk and obscure that premium finish you paid for. Regardless of the winner, Apple manufactures strong watches, but you'll want titanium for resilience, ceramic for long-term polish, and aluminum for a lightweight, less expensive option.

title_en: AI can make tech CEOs’ lives easier. What about everyone else?
title_fa: AI can make tech CEOs’ lives easier. What about everyone else?
excerpt_en: On Equity, we discuss why tech CEO statements can seem so tone deaf.
excerpt_fa: On Equity, we discuss why tech CEO statements can seem so tone deaf.
content_en:
Dazzle AI CEO Marissa Mayer recently became the latest tech CEO to face criticism over seemingly out-of-touch comments extolling the usefulness of AI.
In Mayer’s case, that involved asking an AI tool for help with a school-assigned description of her daughter. For OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, that’s included suggesting that parents create personalized podcasts for their kids’ drive to school and also declaring that he could not imagine parenting without ChatGPT. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has even suggested that it will become increasingly acceptable to meet your social and romantic needs through AI.
This all led TechCrunch’s Amanda Silberling to wonder if AI executives are simply too out-of-touch to build products for normal people — a crucial question with Anthropic set to go public just as Wall Street begins losing its appetite for heavy AI spending.
On the latest episode of the Equity podcast, Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I chatted with Amanda about why industry leaders can sometimes seem so tone deaf. Kirsten wondered if this is more of a marketing problem or a product problem.
Amanda’s answer: “A little bit of both.” She also argued that the tech industry is increasingly pushing a future “where basic human interaction gets more and more optimized out of actually occurring,” adding, “And call me old school, but I think that humans being able to talk to each other is probably a net positive for society.”
Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.
Anthony Ha: There’s a lot of societal skepticism about AI, this feeling that the people running these companies don’t have our best interests at heart, that they’re out of touch. And so, you would just think, “Maybe don’t make statements like that,” because of course, people are going to see them very skeptically.
I think [CEOs] are trying to walk this delicate balance. On the one hand, there’s a tremendous financial incentive for them to make the case that you should use this technology in every aspect of your lives. But when you make that case, it actually [doesn’t paint] a very appealing picture. In some cases, it’s downright dystopian.
Kirsten Korosec: Anthony, if they took your advice, we would have nothing to talk about on this show.
But I will say this: There’s this whole idea of ChatGPT and other AI tools making your life easier when it comes to personal relationships. And in many of these cases, it just seems to overcomplicate what would be, like, observing your child. That might be hard for some people, the people who are building these products, and it doesn’t necessarily relate to everyone else out there in the world. It can just seem so incredibly disconnected when you see these quotes.
To me, it always comes back to — who are they speaking to? Are there people out there who can relate? Maybe there are.
Amanda Silberling: Other use cases we’ve seen people mention are, like, the Bumble CEO Whitney Wolf Heard has made comments about, “Well, what if we had AI concierges, your AI dates the other person’s AI. And then if the AIs have a good date together, then they introduce the people.”
Or in the New York Times article, Marissa Mayer mentioned, “Well, what if my AI could coordinate with my husband’s AI” and stuff like that. And I think that it feels like people are trying to over-optimize out of just having conversations with people.
I’ve already seen that happen in my generation, where I do notice in myself that if I’m ordering takeout, it feels weird to call a place. I’m just so used to, “Well, obviously you can do it online and you don’t have to talk to anyone. And I feel like there’s just going to be more of these things, where basic human interaction gets more and more optimized out of actually occurring. And call me old school, but I think that humans being able to talk to each other is probably a net positive for society.
Sean O’Kane: Yeah, but what’s the ROI, Amanda? How much revenue can you generate off of a conversation that somebody’s having in meatspace?
Amanda: That is the thing, though. Dating is really inefficient. It sucks that you have to go on a bunch of dates with different people. You might waste an evening and be like, “Well, that was a bust.” And so you can see why people are [wondering,] “What if you didn’t have to go on dates? What if your AI could go on dates for you?” But there’s just something not human there.
And then also, you are outsourcing the decision of who you are going to date to a computer that you are trusting knows you better than yourself, which I don’t think is true.
Kirsten: One thing that I think is worth going back to, and I sort of hinted about this earlier: Who are they talking to? Who is their audience for all these optimizations, in your view? Is it a product problem, or is it a messaging problem? Are they just talking about it in the wrong way, and actually, there’s this really great value in here and it just seems out of touch with reality and humanity, but if they just talked about it differently, it would be better? Or is it actually a product problem, and to your point, that we’re focusing on optimizing sort of the wrong things with AI tools?
Amanda: I think it’s a little bit of both, but I think that the marketing problem comes from when you have these high-up people at these massively valuable companies in a room together, talking about the pain points in their lives, and [they focus on] making dinner reservations, booking flights. Everybody does those things, but I’m not booking flights once a week. I’m not making dinner reservations all the time. And when I do, those aren’t really things that I find to be a particular challenge in my life.
I mean, obviously people find value from things like ChatGPT and Claude, but I think the value that the average person is finding isn’t necessarily like booking a flight for me.
Anthony: One of the things I’ve also been thinking about is, there are companies like Uber that, when it first launched, it was...

title_en: How to know if a USB-C cable is waterproof
title_fa: How to know if a USB-C cable is waterproof
excerpt_en: If you need extra protection for your USB cables, knowing how to tell if they're waterproof beforehand is important. Here's how to check a cable's rating.
excerpt_fa: If you need extra protection for your USB cables, knowing how to tell if they're waterproof beforehand is important. Here's how to check a cable's rating.
content_en:
How to know if a USB-C cable is waterproof
Always check the IP rating when purchasing a waterproof USB-C cable
Some USB-C cables are waterproof, but you need to learn to recognize which ones. Widely available from online retailers, including Amazon, they're likely to feature seals to protect the connection and ship in a variety of types, including male, female, and angled cables. But do the seals work? The International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) has developed the IEC 60529 standard, a globally accepted Ingress Protection code that shows how well an enclosure (such as a USB-C plug) resists solids and liquids.
The first number in this code represents dust protection, while the second shows water protection. Under this code, waterproof USB-C cables should have an IP67 or IP68 rating. These cables are most frequently used in specific tough environments, such as manufacturing, construction, maritime and electric vehicle charging systems — anywhere exposed to water, weather or accident. When choosing a cable, what matters most is the IP rating (even for other gadgets, like your phone):
- IP67: A dust-tight cable that can handle being under up to one meter of water for up to 30 minutes.
- IP68: A dust-tight cable suitable for continuous immersion, typically beyond 1 meter, though this varies by manufacturer.
What are the risks of USB water exposure?
The USB-C standard does not specify water resistance, which means that while ordinary cables may survive a splash, nothing is guaranteed and water exposure comes with some risks. USB-C is versatile, ubiquitous and complex. Take a connector apart, and you'll find it contains 24 contacts, which may connect to data or power wires inside the cable. (That's 20 more pins than found in USB-A, which helps account for the faster data transfers.) If water gets inside the connector, it can cause a short circuit that may damage your equipment, while long-term moisture exposure can corrode contacts. There's also the risk that short-circuited wet cables can overheat, potentially causing a fire. You should never plug a wet cable — even a waterproof one — into a device.
USB cable protection is usually achieved with a silicone rubber seal, gasket, or locking collar around the connector to protect against water ingress. Some rely on threaded bayonet couplings, with a rubber seal that compresses as the collar is tightened, creating a watertight link. Cables designed for extended water exposure may use a tough synthetic rubber, such as neoprene. An even tougher material called fluoroelastomer (FKM) is frequently used where chemical or solvent resistance is required.
Can you use a wet cable once it dries?
If the contacts show no corrosion, you can generally use the cable safely again once it dries. To dry a cable, unplug it, shake the connector ends to force water out, and let it dry for 24 to 48 hours. Don't try to dry the cable with a hair dryer, as the heat can damage the cable, and don't use rice, as it can introduce grit and dust into the connector. If a cable becomes hot when using it after drying, replace it.
Brands of waterproof cables, such as Atlavox, Yale, and the more industrial-grade L-Com, are available at good DIY/tech retailers and also at Amazon. You should ensure the cable you choose is IP-rated, rather than simply being water resistant. Basic waterproof cables are available for around ten dollars, while ultra-rugged waterproof cables for the toughest environments can cost ten times that. Finally, when purchasing one of these cables, you should always check the official IP rating, as a cable that doesn't provide this may not deliver what you need.
