title_en: Flock keeps ignoring requests to cancel its contracts
title_fa: Flock keeps ignoring requests to cancel its contracts
excerpt_en: While more cities are canceling their contracts with Flock Safety, just as many are discovering how difficult that can be in some instances. Plymouth, Minnesota's city council voted to terminate its contract with Flock in September, but failed to respond to the city's request....
excerpt_fa: While more cities are canceling their contracts with Flock Safety, just as many are discovering how difficult that can be in some instances. Plymouth, Minnesota's city council voted to terminate its contract with Flock in September, but failed to respond to the city's request....
content_en:
While more cities are canceling their contracts with Flock Safety, just as many are discovering how difficult that can be in some instances. Plymouth, Minnesota’s city council voted to terminate its contract with Flock in September, but failed to respond to the city’s request. For over a month, the cameras remained up, and the city had received no acknowledgment from the company. So, Police Chief Eric Fadden took matters into his own hands and physically disconnected the cameras.
Flock keeps ignoring requests to cancel its contracts
Cities are canceling Flock contracts, but the company won’t take them down and sometimes is reinstalling them.
Cities are canceling Flock contracts, but the company won’t take them down and sometimes is reinstalling them.
“After hearing nothing for more than a week, I directed our staff to disconnect the power cords from the cameras in order to be sure that they are not functioning or recording plates,” Fadden told The Drive.
Roughly 20 miles up the road, Dayton, Minnesota, is having its own issues with Flock. In this instance, the company acknowledged the city’s request and said it would take up to 60 days to remove the equipment. Despite this, Flock reconnected two cameras within the city limits without authorization, and following a specific request from the local police not to complete the work order.
Dayton’s local government posted on Facebook:
On September 17, 2026, the Police Department was made aware of a maintenance work order produced by Flock. The City notified Flock on September 18, 2026, that the program was on hold, and no work orders were to be completed. Unfortunately, the City’s direction was not followed, and the camera was placed back into service without authorization.
Flock spokesperson Andrew Smith told The Verge, “We are proud of the impact our technology has had in Plymouth. We respect the city’s decision and are working with the customer to have the cameras removed.”
This follows a similar ordeal in Illinois, where the company refused to take down cameras and uncovered cameras at Elgin Community College after the administration sought to cancel its contract.
Update November 1st: Added comment from Flock.

title_en: 5 ways to get Amazon Prime for free (or way cheaper)
title_fa: 5 ways to get Amazon Prime for free (or way cheaper)
excerpt_en: Don't pay full price; you might already qualify for cheaper Prime or have another benefit that covers the membership fee
excerpt_fa: Don't pay full price; you might already qualify for cheaper Prime or have another benefit that covers the membership fee
content_en:
5 ways to get Amazon Prime for free (or way cheaper)
Amazon's free trials are only the beginning.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
It's easy to justify the price of Amazon Prime when you take advantage of Prime Day deals or have a gift delivered tomorrow, just in time. But when you've paid another $14.99 and only bought a USB cable this month, the numbers are not as attractive.
If Prime's sticker price is a no-go for you, you might be able to get away with paying less. You may qualify for six months of Amazon Prime at no cost. There are also discounted Prime plans that cost half as much as a regular monthly membership, or even less. You could also have the option to get Prime through someone in your household, your employer or a benefit bundled with another service.
Start with Amazon's free trials and discounted plans
If you qualify, Amazon's standard 30-day free trial is the simplest way to get Prime at no cost. With this trial period, you'll receive Prime benefits like fast shipping, exclusive discounts on some products, improved Alexa and access to Prime Video, all without having to pay any initial subscription fee. This can be especially useful if you're joining prior to Prime Day or in preparation for the holiday shopping season where a single month of service is enough.
Amazon requires a payment method and automatically converts the trial into a paid subscription unless you cancel your Amazon Prime membership before renewal. Amazon also doesn't specify a waiting period before former subscribers qualify for another free trial. Therefore, you shouldn't count on receiving free Prime each year during the shopping season.
Other plans provide different ways to save. Prime for Young Adults gives eligible new members six months of free service. Afterward, they can choose to pay $7.49 monthly or $69 annually. Eligibility covers adults ages 18 to 24, as well as higher-education students of any age. To qualify, you must provide proof of your age or school enrollment.
Prime Access costs $6.99 per month after a 30-day free trial for eligible new members receiving qualifying government assistance or meeting Amazon's income requirements. It includes all the same perks as the standard Prime membership, and is open to SNAP or Medicaid recipients. Double-check your eligibility, since current Prime members may be able to transition to the discounted membership.
Share Prime benefits through Amazon Family
If someone in your household already pays for Prime, chances are you don't need a second membership. Amazon Family lets a paying subscriber share select Prime benefits (including fast shipping, exclusive shopping deals and ad-supported Prime Video) with another adult living at the same primary address. Each adult keeps a separate Amazon account, so there's no need to borrow login credentials to place an order.
There's a privacy tradeoff, though: Amazon requires the family organizer to share a payment method that the other adult can use for purchases. Before sending an invitation, review your payment, digital content and order history sharing settings.
Also, the program limits who can participate. In October 2025, Amazon ended its Prime Invitee program, which previously allowed members to share free shipping with people outside their household. Friends at another address can no longer receive your free shipping benefit through that program. Note that free trial and Prime for Young Adults members cannot share their Prime benefits through Amazon Family.
Check your work benefits, phone plan and credit card perks
Free Prime memberships are available to eligible US employees at Amazon, while Whole Foods announced that its hourly workers will receive the same benefit beginning January 1, 2027. If you work for either company, checking your benefits could save you from paying for Prime twice.
Metro by T-Mobile began bundling Prime with select plans in 2018, but stopped offering the perk to new customers on September 17, 2026. Eligible legacy customers can still keep it, so before you switch carriers or make adjustments to your plan, check what your existing setup includes. You could potentially lose out on a free membership if you change.
Existing Navy Federal Visa Signature Flagship Rewards cardholders receive a $139 statement credit toward an annual Amazon Prime membership paid with the card, but that's no longer open to new applicants. It's been replaced by the newer Flagship Premier card, which offers a $100 airline credit instead.
If you have the Flagship Rewards card, be aware that the annual fee increased from $49 to $95 on November 2, 2026. After that, the net annual savings from the Prime credit will be $44 if you count no other card benefits. According to Navy Federal, it may take six to eight weeks for the statement credit to appear on your account.
There are other offbeat methods to getting a lower-cost Prime subscription. Programs like Microsoft Rewards give you points that you can redeem toward gift cards, including Amazon gift cards to put towards Prime. If you're a frequent Amazon shopper, the Amazon Prime Visa grants five percent back on all Amazon purchases with Prime, which can help cover the cost of a subscription. And low-income customers who qualify for Spectrum's Internet Assist plan can get Amazon Prime for no extra cost.

title_en: How to turn on the flashlight on your Android phone without unlocking it
title_fa: How to turn on the flashlight on your Android phone without unlocking it
excerpt_en: You can easily access your flashlight on Samsung Galaxy and Google Pixel devices - here's how.
excerpt_fa: You can easily access your flashlight on Samsung Galaxy and Google Pixel devices - here's how.
content_en:
How to turn on the flashlight on your Android phone without unlocking it
Quickly access your flashlight on Samsung Galaxy and Google Pixel phones.
You don't have to unlock your Android phone to switch your flashlight on. There are shortcuts so you can easily and quickly access it in case of emergency. In this post, we'll focus on Samsung Galaxy and Google Pixel phones, both of which have a customizable pulldown menu from the lock screen where you'll find a slew of useful tools.
If you want to go the hands-free route, you can also you can ask your AI assistant to turn on the flashlight for you in both cases. Start by saying "Hey, Google" without unlocking your phone and then follow it up with "Turn on the flashlight."
Google Pixel
You can find the flashlight button on your Pixel phone by swiping down from the top of the screen to bring up the Quick Settings menu. Just tap on the flashlight icon to switch it on, then tap it again to switch it off. If you can't find it among the top options in Quick Settings, you'll have to edit the icons in the first page. Simply tap on the pencil at the bottom of the Quick Settings menu and then press the plus button on the Flashlight icon and/or move it to the top of the menu so you can see it quickly whenever you need it.
While you can't shake the Pixel to switch the Flashlight on — that's an old Motorola feature — you can set your phone's Quick Tap gesture to activate it. Go to Settings > System > Gestures > Quick Tap to start actions and then enable Toggle Flashlight from there. After setting that up, you'll be able to turn your flashlight on by double tapping the back of your phone. You can, however, find third-party apps that will give you the ability to turn the flashlight on by shaking your device.
It's also possible to edit your phone's lock screen buttons by long pressing on your lock screen and then tapping on the Customize button at the bottom. Scroll down to find the Shortcuts option and then choose the flashlight icon to add it to the bottom of your lock screen.
Samsung Galaxy phones
On Samsung Galaxy phones, you can easily access your flashlight through the Quick Panel, which you can see by swiping down from either corner of the top of your screen. If you don't see it there or want to reorder the icons in the panel, just tap on the kebab or the pencil icon while it's open. You'll be able to edit the panel from there and rearrange the icons as you see fit.
You can change the two buttons and the bottom corners of your lock screen, as well. Typically, those two buttons are the Phone and Camera icons, but you can switch out one of them by long pressing anywhere on the lock screen. Choose from one of them and then select the flashlight to replace it. If you can't seem to customize your lock screen, go to Settings > Lock Screen & AOD > Enable Touch and Hold to Edit.

title_en: Judge says xAI must face NAACP lawsuit on data center pollution
title_fa: Judge says xAI must face NAACP lawsuit on data center pollution
excerpt_en: The legal battle revolves around the AI company's operations in southern Memphis.
excerpt_fa: The legal battle revolves around the AI company's operations in southern Memphis.
content_en:
Judge says xAI must face NAACP lawsuit on data center pollution
The legal battle revolves around the AI company’s operations in southern Memphis.
A federal judge's latest ruling has denied xAI's request to dismiss a lawsuit that alleges its data center campus in Memphis, Tennessee is running turbines without proper permits and violating the Clean Air Act. The decision, from US District Judge Debra M. Brown, allows the lawsuit, which was filed by the NAACP, to move forward.
The organization filed its legal action against xAI in April, accusing the company that's now known as SpaceXSI of using unpermitted methane gas turbines to power data centers in the Memphis area. Despite the ongoing lawsuit that also claimed it's violating the Clear Air Act, Elon Musk's company continued to add more gas turbines to another AI data center site in the nearby Southhaven, Mississippi community. In response, xAI requested to dismiss the NAACP lawsuit and even received support from the Justice Department, which claimed that the company's operations are a crucial part of US military operations.
xAI said the lawsuit should be dismissed, claiming that its turbines were exempt from permitting requirements since they were mobile. Judge Brown wrote in her decision that the power plant where all the turbines were providing power to xAI's data center wasn't mobile and therefore not exempt from the permitting process. The lawsuit comes at a time when AI companies are ramping up the construction of data centers to fuel their AI needs, while neighbors are becoming increasingly averse to these buildouts.

title_en: This hidden Windows 11 menu can save you valuable time when troubleshooting
title_fa: This hidden Windows 11 menu can save you valuable time when troubleshooting
excerpt_en: Windows 11 has a sneaky menu that connects you with Settings, Task Manager, Event Viewer, and more in one place.
excerpt_fa: Windows 11 has a sneaky menu that connects you with Settings, Task Manager, Event Viewer, and more in one place.
content_en:
This hidden Windows 11 menu can save you valuable time when troubleshooting
Windows 11 has a sneaky menu that connects you with key tools.
Windows 11 is full of little menus that allow you to manage your computer's processes, optimize its systems and troubleshoot any potential errors. However, it can be a nuisance to know all the right hotkeys and where to look for some of the more obscure areas of your device. Luckily, one of the easiest ways to debloat and manage Windows 11 is with a hidden menu you may not have heard of.
This hidden menu goes by a few names, including both the Quick Link Menu and the Windows-X Menu. The latter name is in reference to how you find this secret area, which is by hitting the Win+X keys. Hitting those buttons and opening that menu will allow you to parse a curated selection of other menus and options — granting you access to a myriad of management options in one place.
How to access the Quick Link Menu
If you want to take a glance at this Quick Link Menu, just hit those aforementioned Win+X keys. The menu will then pop up on the left side of your screen, right above where the Windows logo resides on the taskbar. This will reveal a few of the standard features you'll usually find in the Start menu or pinned to the taskbar — such as Settings, File Explorer, Search, Shutdown options and so on. However, you'll also find a number of features usually buried in your Settings (including Installed Apps, System, Power Options and Network Connections) or behind other hotkeys (such as Mobility Center, Event Viewer, Disk Management, Computer Management and Task Manager).
You can also customize this Quick Link layout by heading to File Explorer and type %LOCALAPPDATA%MicrosoftWindowsWinX into the address bar. The three folders kept in this area store the shortcuts found in the menu, and you can move the shortcuts around them. You can also rename the apps by renaming these shortcuts, and can add new shortcuts by dragging apps from elsewhere in the File Explorer and into one of these folders.
The best troubleshooting tools in the Quick Link Menu
Those non-Settings options are especially important, as using Windows-X here allows you to forgo memorizing many hotkeys and access some excellent menu features. title_en: The biggest problem with trying to directly power EVs with solar roofs
title_fa: The biggest problem with trying to directly power EVs with solar roofs
excerpt_en: Solar roofs promise a future where EVs rarely need plugging in, but turning that vision into reality presents some surprisingly difficult challenges.
excerpt_fa: Solar roofs promise a future where EVs rarely need plugging in, but turning that vision into reality presents some surprisingly difficult challenges.
content_en:
The biggest problem with trying to directly power EVs with solar roofs
A car roof can only catch so much sunlight, and adding more panels brings its own problems.
A solar roof seems like an ideal EV accessory. Park outside, skip plugging it in, and drive away with a full battery. The problem is that even a relatively large car roof provides little room to harvest solar energy, and driving a modern EV requires significant electricity.
You might think to add more panels. However, additional hardware hinders the car in more ways than one. Added weight requires electric motors to work harder and thus draw more energy. Furthermore, extra hardware can compromise aerodynamics, increasing drag and lowering efficiency.
Car makers are attempting to overcome these limitations by testing solar panels that can be stretched when a vehicle is parked, along with light EVs that can go further on each watt-hour. However, implementing these concepts comes with practical challenges, which we'll explore.
In comparison, RVs are better suited to rooftop solar since panels (such as Winnebago's 210W system on the Revel Sport) can be used to power lights, fans and refrigerators. They're not expected to help move the vehicle.
A solar roof can only generate so much electricity
Begin with the numbers. The EPA estimates the median model-year 2025 EV uses 39kWh per 100 miles, or 390Wh per mile. Let's assume that a 400W solar array is mounted on approximately 22 square feet of an EV's roof. If it generated its rated output for four hours, it would only produce 1.6kWh before charging losses. This is sufficient energy for approximately 4 miles at the EPA's average consumption rate.
And that's assuming favorable conditions. Shade, cloudy weather, heat and unfavorable parking angles can all reduce solar output. You also have limited roof space. Still, we can't help but think of Squad Mobility's tiny solar-powered EV, which pairs a 250W roof panel with a 794-pound city car.
Larger arrays add weight and may increase aerodynamic drag, especially when mounted above the bodywork. Panels that are integrated flush with the roof can largely avoid the aerodynamic penalty, but not the space issue. The compromise is demonstrated in Nissan's Ao-Solar Extender prototype for its Sakura EV, which generates up to 300W with the panel retracted for driving. When the car is parked, an extra panel slides over the windshield to increase the output to 500W. The expandable configuration provides Nissan with more collecting area without a big panel protruding at highway speeds.
Aptera's solution is a very different kind of EV
Instead of attempting to cram a massive solar panel on a traditional vehicle, Aptera has designed an EV featuring a teardrop-shaped body with three wheels, just two seats and lightweight composite construction. That's quite different from the median model-year 2025 EV. Aptera is aiming for 100Wh per mile, which is about a fourth of the EPA's median EV consumption.
Aptera's solar panels have delivered measurable results. During July testing in Southern California, TÜV Rheinland measured 4.23kWh delivered to an Aptera prototype's battery, with the car parked, untouched and its hatch closed. At Aptera's targeted efficiency, that equates to about 42 miles of solar range. That could translate to plugging in less often for someone who has a short commute and a sunny parking spot. Still, garage parking, a few days of cloudy skies or a long road trip alters the equation. The test also confirmed the electricity collected, not how far the car could actually drive on it.
History has shown that Aptera's goal isn't easy. For example, Lightyear suspended production of its first solar EV in January 2023, just weeks after deliveries began. Lightyear's operating company, Atlas Technologies, entered bankruptcy days later.
Aptera has yet to announce a final selling price, but the Launch Edition has a target price of $40,000. The company says in its October 1 SEC filing that it plans to begin building its first 40 production vehicles by the end of 2026, with customer deliveries expected in early 2027, subject to financing, supplier performance and regulatory approvals.

title_en: How much would it cost to build a PC similar to the Xbox Series S?
title_fa: How much would it cost to build a PC similar to the Xbox Series S?
excerpt_en: The Xbox Series S offers a solid entry-level experience for those interested in console gaming. Here's what an equivalent gaming PC would cost you.
excerpt_fa: The Xbox Series S offers a solid entry-level experience for those interested in console gaming. Here's what an equivalent gaming PC would cost you.
content_en:
How much would it cost to build a PC similar to the Xbox Series S?
It's not too hard to build a PC that plays the same role as the Xbox Series S, but it won't necessarily come cheap.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
Microsoft markets the Xbox Series S as a value pick for console gamers, running games at 1440p and up to 120 FPS. Its hardware may be a bit dated, and even the 512GB base model runs $500 after recent price hikes, but PCs aren't cheap either now, as AI's demand for computer hardware continues to drive consumer hardware prices ever higher. Even old GPUs are now valuable.
But an Xbox is limited to gaming and media consumption, so it still makes sense to try and build a Series S equivalent in 2026. However, the Series S' older, custom hardware means there's no apples-to-apples comparison for current-generation custom PC builds. You could use older parts, but you'd be better off buying the Xbox in that case. Older parts make sense in a console that developers are actively optimizing their games for, but a PC won't be as accommodating. The good news, though, is that it's not hard to build a computer that crushes the budget Xbox on paper and offers a similarly enjoyable entry-level PC gaming experience. The predictable trade-off is that it will also crush your wallet.
My criteria for this theoretical build were simple. It had to outperform the Xbox Series S running at 1080p native (or 1440p with reduced settings and upscaling) and could only use parts you can still buy from major retailers. Refurbished parts were ruled out, since those deals might be gone by the time you read this. That said, PC part pricing has never been as volatile as it is right now, so consider this a snapshot of the current market rather than a guide that'll serve you well years from now.
CPU, motherboard, and RAM
The Xbox Series S has an AMD Zen 2-based CPU with 8 physical cores clocked at 3.6GHz, which ramps down to 3.4GHz in multi-threaded tasks. Its RDNA2 GPU has 12 compute units and runs at 1,565MHz. Memory is unified across the system, so the entire machine shares 10GB of GDDR6 RAM on a 128-bit-wide bus with 2.4GB/s of raw throughput. In plain English, it's an entry-level configuration. However, like other consoles, the Series S is tuned for gaming performance at all costs and punches above its weight class in real-world use.
To keep things as even as possible, we'll go with an AMD CPU and GPU for our PC. The first decision is between AM4 and AM5. The newer socket is more future-proof, but we'll go with AM4 to save money on the motherboard and RAM while still getting a better CPU than the Zen 2 component found in the Series S. The budget pick is a Ryzen 5 5600, available for around $160 on Amazon at the time of writing. The flex pick is the Ryzen 5 5600X3D, which has better gaming performance thanks to its larger L3 cache. It often goes on sale for around $175 and is a good deal at that price.
AM4 lets us run DDR4 RAM instead of DDR5, which is a huge relief for our budget. Building on the B550M chipset will set us back $80-$90, though sales do occur regularly. To ensure we get VRM heatsinks and no PCIe-related bottlenecks, we'll go with the ASRock B550M Phantom Gaming 4. It may need a BIOS update to support the Ryzen 5 5600, but should work well afterward.
While it's easy to assume we'll only need a single 8GB stick of RAM, alongside our chosen GPU's VRAM, to beat out the Xbox Series S' 10GB of unified system memory, Ryzen performs better with dual-channel memory. We'll use two 4GB sticks instead. Lenovo's 2x4GB DDR4 kit runs at a respectable 3,200MT/s and costs just $40. It's admittedly not a high-performance kit, but it should still help our build outperform the Series S without breaking the bank.
GPU and other components
Picking a GPU is a bit more difficult. The closest equivalent is the NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1060 from 2019, but that would be a terrible choice since it's too old to support newer titles. Another good choice might be the GeForce RTX 3050, which is around $250, but its 6GB of VRAM likely isn't enough for modern gaming. To reduce the risk of VRAM-related issues, we'll instead go with the ASRock Challenger Radeon RX 7600 8GB, which offers significantly better performance than the Xbox Series S on paper and can be had for $330.
Two other valid options are the single-fan RTX 5050, which currently retails for around $300, or the Intel Arc B570, which costs about $290 and has a respectable 10GB of VRAM. We'll go with the AMD to better match the Xbox's all-AMD design and avoid any driver or support-related headaches that may arise with the Intel part.
We still need to choose a CPU cooler, storage drive, power supply and case. Our cooler is an easy pick, with the Thermalright Peerless Assassin 120 SE available for around $35. For storage, a 512GB SSD on par with or better than the Series S costs about $100. Our power supply is a 600W Thermaltake Toughpower GX2 with plenty of headroom for our 350W TDP and 80+ Gold certification. We should be able to cram the build into a Zalman Cubix-G micro-ATX tower for between $35 and $45, though we may need a cheap adapter to make the front USB-C cable work.
All in, this build will cost roughly $740 before taxes, using the lowest prices available at the time of writing. That's significantly more than the Xbox Series S' current price and over double what the console cost at launch. That said, this build should outperform it and will do more than just play games. Component pricing will vary, of course, and individual builders can also make different trade-offs to hit a lower price point or aim for better performance.

title_en: 5 safety practices to know before vibe coding
title_fa: 5 safety practices to know before vibe coding
excerpt_en: Here's what beginners need to know to vibe code securely.
excerpt_fa: Here's what beginners need to know to vibe code securely.
content_en:
5 safety practices to know before vibe coding
Here’s what beginners need to know to vibe code securely.
The term "vibe coding" has spread across the tech world since early last year, after OpenAI co-founder Andrej Karpathy wrote about his experience of generating code by just talking to an AI model without really thinking about the code itself. "I just see stuff, say stuff, run stuff, and copy paste stuff, and it mostly works," he wrote in the X post that sparked the term.
In the tech industry, vibe coding is now the new normal. While it's a powerful way to move faster with less resources, generating code with AI that you don't fully understand or haven't reviewed can pose serious security risks to yourself, your devices and anyone using your app. The AI app-focused cybersecurity firm Apiiro says it looked into Fortune 50 companies and found that vibe coding makes engineers four times more productive but resulted in ten times the number of security issues. So don't vibe-code without following these basic security best practices.
1. Be specific in the prompt and make a markdown file
Treat the AI model like you would a lazy genie. Many AI models will take quick shortcuts to technically deliver what you asked for but without implementing safety measures or double-checking work. Don't assume the AI will keep critical information private, implement cybersecurity best practices or check its code for potential exploits.
Spell out what you want with as much specificity as possible, including privacy specs, limitations on who can access what part of what you're creating and other security guardrails and protections you want added to the project, like encryption. You can also ask it to reference the OWASP list of top vulnerabilities to help avoid these issues before the code has even been written.
Most AI models will give you the ability to make persistent rules or context files, so you don't have to repeat the same instructions every time you sit down to build. Create a markdown file (.md file) with any AI model or add information to the "Knowledge" section in the Lovable agent or the "Memory" section if you're using Replit. AI markdown files are useful for adding safety guidelines because the AI will consider the file's instructions with every prompt or task. And before getting started, choosing vibe-coding tools that support audit logs can help you track every change to your project more easily.
2. Keep API keys and passwords out of the chat (and code)
It's never a good idea to put API keys or passwords directly into an AI prompt. This type of sensitive data should never show up in the code, either, because if you push your code to Github later, all that critical info will be available for anyone to see. Limiting what your AI tool has access to can also help prevent prompt injection attacks.
Instead, store sensitive data in a dedicated password manager and use the "environmental variables" or "secrets" tabs on Replit, Lovable or Vercel. This is the easiest and best method for total beginners.
If the AI tool you're using doesn't have a feature like this built-in already, you will have to make a backend "environmental variable" .env file for this data and make sure that file does not get made public at any stage in the process. This means making it part of a .gitignore file and ensuring it is never visible on the app or website's frontend.
To check if you've done this correctly, you can use TruffleHog, a tool that will check your code to make sure you haven't accidentally leaked sensitive info.
3. Protect the app data
If you're building anything that will involve lots of data, it may involve the use of a type of Structured Query Language, or SQL, to handle this information. Consumer apps like Spotify, for example, use SQL to optimize app performance when transmitting data to the user. Vulnerable SQL databases can lead to SQL injection attacks, allowing hackers to swipe or delete that data and replace it with whatever they want.
Tell the AI to parameterize queries, sanitize inputs, use Server Actions for critical actions, enable row-level security (RLS) and create RLS policies if applicable. All of these tactics make code harder to exploit and protect your app data.
It's also good practice to make sure the AI is using the latest versions of existing libraries. AI has also hallucinated the existence of packages that aren't real or might use malicious ones by accident, so keep an eye out for this as well.
4. Rate limiting is your friend
If you've ever heard about DDoS attacks, rate limiting is one way to help protect your app from falling victim to one. Rate limiting can prevent them by limiting how many times someone (or a bot) can do a specific action.
Password attempt rate-limiting can prevent brute-force attacks and credential-stuffing. How much you'll want to rate-limit depends on what your vibe app does. If it's a free app like a support chatbot, rate-limiting could save your bank account by limiting how many tokens can be used per day per user. If possible, rate-limit by account ID first and then by IP address. This way, hackers can't spam as easily and your rate-limiting can't be circumvented with VPN use.
Email or phone authentication flows and CAPTCHA are other good steps to add to your app to help prevent unwanted activity.
5. Review and test the AI's work
If you can't get a professional software engineer to review your vibe-coded project, ask the AI to evaluate its own work for potential exploits, including testing it against the OWASP Top 10 risks even if you had it look at these earlier. Then, use other AI models to look for potential issues.
There are also a number of tools that can evaluate vibe-coded projects including Claude Code Security, Codex Security, Stackhawk's Wingman, CheckVibe, SafeToShip and the Vibe App Scanner. But quashing bugs doesn't stop after you ship, so you'll have to monitor your vibe app or site for issues to stay safe.

If you're building anything that will involve lots of data, it may involve the use of a type of Structured Query Language, or SQL, to handle this information. Consumer apps like Spotify, for example, use SQL to optimize app performance when transmitting data to the user. Vulnerable SQL databases can lead to SQL injection attacks, allowing hackers to swipe or delete that data and replace it with whatever they want.
Tell the AI to parameterize queries, sanitize inputs, use Server Actions for critical actions, enable row-level security (RLS) and create RLS policies if applicable. All of these tactics make code harder to exploit and protect your app data.
It's also good practice to make sure the AI is using the latest versions of existing libraries. AI has also hallucinated the existence of packages that aren't real or might use malicious ones by accident, so keep an eye out for this as well.
4. Rate limiting is your friend
If you've ever heard about DDoS attacks, rate limiting is one way to help protect your app from falling victim to one. Rate limiting can prevent them by limiting how many times someone (or a bot) can do a specific action.
Password attempt rate-limiting can prevent brute-force attacks and credential-stuffing. How much you'll want to rate-limit depends on what your vibe app does. If it's a free app like a support chatbot, rate-limiting could save your bank account by limiting how many tokens can be used per day per user. If possible, rate-limit by account ID first and then by IP address. This way, hackers can't spam as easily and your rate-limiting can't be circumvented with VPN use.
Email or phone authentication flows and CAPTCHA are other good steps to add to your app to help prevent unwanted activity.
5. Review and test the AI's work
If you can't get a professional software engineer to review your vibe-coded project, ask the AI to evaluate its own work for potential exploits, including testing it against the OWASP Top 10 risks even if you had it look at these earlier. Then, use other AI models to look for potential issues.
There are also a number of tools that can evaluate vibe-coded projects including Claude Code Security, Codex Security, Stackhawk's Wingman, CheckVibe, SafeToShip and the Vibe App Scanner. But quashing bugs doesn't stop after you ship, so you'll have to monitor your vibe app or site for issues to stay safe.

title_en: Apple’s HomeView could add security camera features
title_fa: Apple’s HomeView could add security camera features
excerpt_en: Reddit user pdfu found hints hidden in the HomeView 27.2 code that Apple could be adding security camera features to its smart home hub. The strings describe a security camera mode with motion detection, live streaming, and recording options, as well as privacy functions....
excerpt_fa: Reddit user pdfu found hints hidden in the HomeView 27.2 code that Apple could be adding security camera features to its smart home hub. The strings describe a security camera mode with motion detection, live streaming, and recording options, as well as privacy functions....
content_en:
Reddit user pdfu found hints hidden in the HomeView 27.2 code that Apple could be adding security camera features to its smart home hub. The strings describe a security camera mode with motion detection, live streaming, and recording options, as well as privacy functions. According to pdfu, there is a setup page that even explicitly reads: “Your HomeView can be used as a security camera with HomeKit Secure Video.”
Apple’s HomeView could add security camera features
Code strings in HomeView’s software suggest Apple could launch a Secure Video feature soon.
Code strings in HomeView’s software suggest Apple could launch a Secure Video feature soon.
Supposedly, the video feeds will only be visible to members of the home, and will both show an indicator light and play a sound when either someone is watching the camera feed or when it starts to record. Home members will also get a notification anytime settings are changed for the Secure Video mode. It will also include customizable options for what to detect, stream, or record, based on whether you’re home, away, or asleep.
Some wondered why Apple did not allow HomeView to double as a security camera at launch, and the company hasn’t said anything to suggest the features are coming. But, considering how central privacy is to Apple’s marketing, the company may be waiting to fine-tune those features before launch.

title_en: TechCrunch Mobility: A new, bigger AV boom is here
title_fa: TechCrunch Mobility: A new, bigger AV boom is here
excerpt_en: Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it.
excerpt_fa: Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it.
content_en:
Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility!
I’ve joked here and on the Equity and Autonocast podcasts that the autonomous vehicle industry feels a lot like 2016, at least in terms of the buzziness surrounding the sector.
But a recent conversation with Trucks VC partner Puneeth Meruva has me rethinking that comparison. There’s evidence that 2026 is even hotter — at least by certain measures — than those frothy dealmaking days of 2016 and 2017.
Trucks VC, which specializes in early-stage investing, has fielded pitches from 81 new autonomous vehicle startups so far in 2026 — two-thirds more than last year and enough to surpass the boom years of a decade ago. The VC firm argues in a new blog post that we’re in the midst of a second, even bigger AV wave fueled by technological breakthroughs. Yes, I’m talking about AI.
“For a long time AV companies were trying to go from what was AV 1.0 to AV 2.0, which is kind of this holy grail end-to-end architecture for AVs,” Meruva told me. “And I think the foundation models now provide a technical architecture that makes those end-to-end systems possible.”
These foundational models are particularly good at generalizing across different environments and scenarios, potentially making AVs cheaper and faster to deploy. The arrival of powerful open source models like Nvidia’s Alpamayo and Qwen’s general-purpose vision-language-action models has made it even easier for startups to get off the ground.
The barrier to entry is lower than ever before. Meruva said Trucks is consistently seeing startups deploy within a few months and with less than $1 million raised. (And while Meruva wouldn’t name names, the firm has invested in some of them.)
Of these 81 startups that pitched Trucks VC, I mistakenly assumed most would be applying their AV tech to construction, warehouse, agriculture, and mining. And yes, those were in the mix. But what surprised me was the growing number of startups pitching pure-play robotaxi businesses. And many are positioning themselves as direct competitors to Waymo.
As wild and galaxy brain-thinking as that may sound, Meruva thinks there is room for smaller players.
“In this world, smaller, more niche autonomy companies can compete — maybe they’re not competing with Waymo on a global scale, but maybe they’re competing in specific regions or specific types of routes,” he said.
And Meruva doesn’t see the pace flattening. He expects even more AV startups to pitch the firm next year.
Deals!
Regular readers of this newsletter know we’ve been closely following Slate Auto — breaking the original story on Jeff Bezos’ investment way back in April 2025. But the company it spun out of is what got our attention this week.
Re:Build, a Massachusetts-based manufacturing accelerator, raised $2.1 billion to “expand Re:Build’s capacity to manufacture hard tech products and launch new industrial startups.” The investment was led by General Catalyst and JPMorganChase’s Strategic Investment Group. Other investors weren’t disclosed.
The company, which was co-founded by Amazon’s former commercial CEO Jeff Wilke, has billed itself as “America’s answer to Shenzhen.”
Other deals …
Bedrock Robotics raised $600 million in a funding round that values the autonomous vehicle technology startup at $4.1 billion. CapitalG and Emergence Capital co-led the Series C round. New investors US Innovative Technology Fund (USIT), Bessemer Venture Partners, and Temasek participated in the round, alongside existing investors 8VC, Georgian, Valor Equity Partners, Xora, Eclipse, Perry Creek Capital, and Nvidia.
DoorDash has agreed to acquire Instacart for $17 billion. Meanwhile, DoorDash noted in its third-quarter earnings that it has, so far, only received a few hundred orders from AI agents.
PreScalar, a San Francisco-based startup developing software and testing infrastructure for factories, raised $7 million in seed funding co-led by Dynamo Ventures and BMW i Ventures, with participation from Blue Wire Capital, Uplift Ventures, and Antler. The startup was founded last year by a trio who had stints at Cruise, Google, Rivian, and Waymo.
Notable reads and other tidbits
Elroy Air, a startup developing autonomous heavy-cargo drones for defense, rapid response, and commercial logistics, hired Jeremy Hux as its CFO in preparation for going public.
Ford announced two new EV chargers that will allow its forthcoming Fathom pickup truck to serve as a battery capable of delivering power to the home or grid.
GM is embracing hybrids now. Times sure have changed! The U.S. automaker is also trying to move past the driver data-selling controversy from several years ago. GM agreed to a $220 million settlement with 36 states (its settlement with California and the Federal Trade Commission happened earlier) to settle allegations that it illegally sold private driving behavior and location information to data brokers.
Kodiak AI will deliver 75 self-driving trucks to freight company DTL Transport starting in 2028. It’s the company’s first binding commercial deal for driverless big rigs that will run on public highways.
Rivian reported its third-quarter earnings, and a few items stood out to us. For one, the new R2 has been successful enough for the company to raise its 2026 delivery guidance by a couple thousands vehicles. Rivian, which had previously expected to deliver between 65,000 and 70,000 EVs this year, bumped up that floor to 67,000. But here is another potentially lucrative development: The $5.8 billion joint venture between Rivian and Volkswagen Group is expanding to include AI assistants. No word yet on whether that means VW will invest even more money into Rivian.
Tesla turns to Turo to boost adoption of Full Self-Driving (Supervised).
Waymo and Toyota have locked in a manufacturing partnership, officially moving them...

title_en: Binance resumes withdrawals following $6.3 billion breach
title_fa: Binance resumes withdrawals following $6.3 billion breach
excerpt_en: The cryptocurrency exchange said it's now covered 95% of the stolen assets.
excerpt_fa: The cryptocurrency exchange said it's now covered 95% of the stolen assets.
content_en:
Cryptocurrency exchange Binance announced early on Sunday that it would begin allowing withdrawals in a phased process.
The company froze all deposits and withdrawals after hackers stole $6.3 billion worth of crypto from Binance wallets. In its latest update, Binance said it has now covered 95% of the stolen assets, and it’s still working to buy the “remaining affected assets,” which are “less liquid in the market and take longer time to source at the required scale.”
“Our commitment remains unchanged: Binance will bear the financial impact of the stolen funds,” the company added. “These losses will not be passed on to users.”
As for the withdrawal freeze, Binance said it did not make the decision lightly, as it understands “how important reliable access to withdrawals is for our users.” Nonetheless, the company said this was a necessary “precaution while our teams worked to contain the incident loss, assess its impact, restore affected services, and complete security checks.”
Binance will resume supporting withdrawals in phases, depending on network and asset type. As of Sunday morning, the company’s network status page showed a mix of normal, partially suspended, and fully suspended statuses — for example, Bitcoin withdrawals and deposits are still listed as partially suspended, while Ethereum deposits are normal and withdrawals are partially suspended.
The company also said users should expect “temporary delays or longer processing times due to traffic volume.”
“Resuming withdrawals is a major milestone, but our work continues,” Binance said. “We will continue strengthening our safeguards, completing the recovery process, and providing updates as progress continues.”
Binance subsequently shared that between 6am and 3:30pm Coordinated Universal Time, it processed $4.6 billion in withdrawals and $1.0 billion in deposits, for a net outflow of $3.6 billion — 2.1% of its total assets under management.
The company also said it will publish a more in-depth incident report when its investigation is complete.
Binance previously blamed North Korea hackers for the breach. On Saturday, the FBI said that a North Korean group known as TraderTraitor was responsible, and that the group was converting the assets primarily into Ethereum, with further laundering likely.
This post has been updated with information about net outflows during the initial withdrawal period.

title_fa: A fully playable version of Portal prequel F-Stop leaked
excerpt_en: Leakers have pieced together a playable version of the canceled Portal prequel F-Stop. Most of the assets came from the massive 12-terabyte leak that dropped this August. That didn't include the game's source code or map data, but those final pieces apparently hit the Valve Cut...
excerpt_fa: Leakers have pieced together a playable version of the canceled Portal prequel F-Stop. Most of the assets came from the massive 12-terabyte leak that dropped this August. That didn't include the game's source code or map data, but those final pieces apparently hit the Valve Cut...
content_en:
Leakers have pieced together a playable version of the canceled Portal prequel F-Stop. Most of the assets came from the massive 12-terabyte leak that dropped this August. That didn’t include the game’s source code or map data, but those final pieces apparently hit the Valve Cut Content Discord this week, allowing a nearly complete version to be pieced together.
A fully playable version of Portal prequel F-Stop leaked
Nearly 20 years after it was canceled, the camera-based Portal prequel F-Stop is no longer lost media.
Nearly 20 years after it was canceled, the camera-based Portal prequel F-Stop is no longer lost media.
Some dialog and elements of F-Stop eventually found their way into Portal 2. But it differs dramatically from the mainline Portal games in that it’s built around a camera mechanic that lets you capture an item by taking its picture and place it elsewhere using the resulting Polaroid-like photos. It’s not unlike Viewfinder in that way.
The game is short, with videos showing off its full campaign all clocking in at under an hour. That’s not terribly surprising, though. F-Stop was developed as part of the “Directed Design Experiments,” a three-month period in 2007 when Valve broke into five teams to build new video game experiments.

title_en: Pixel 11 Pro Fold: Sturdy rectangle in a wide wide world
title_fa: Pixel 11 Pro Fold: Sturdy rectangle in a wide wide world
excerpt_en: Google made a sturdy phone, but there is increasing competition in the foldable world.
excerpt_fa: Google made a sturdy phone, but there is increasing competition in the foldable world.
content_en:
It’s strange to write this review when the world is focused on the passport-sized iPhone Duo, and China-based companies are busy releasing wide foldables with a similar design. Google, however, stuck to its guns this year and produced a Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which is pretty much similar to last year’s foldable.
The changes involve a lighter design, a brighter display, better wireless charging, and an updated camera sensor. The new olive color looks subtle but gorgeous, so that’s a bonus. However, with all the options out there, the device might not attract people who might be looking to buy their first foldable — unless they’re serious Pixel fans.
Nonetheless, I have enjoyed using the device because the Pixel 11 Pro Fold’s cameras are competent enough, even if they aren’t a match for the Pixel 11 Pro’s setup, and the screen is nice to use despite the very visible crease.
Design
The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is 5mm thick when unfolded (vs 5.2mm of the Pixel 10 Pro Fold) and 10.1mm thick when folded (vs 10.8 mm of the Pixel 10 Pro Fold). This one is for the spec sheet because you might not feel as much difference. Despite this, the phone is not as thin as a device like the Honor V6 Magic.
The difference you might notice — if you hold both this year’s and last year’s foldables — is that the new device is 19 grams lighter. But if you are buying a new device or switching from another foldable, it’s barely noticeable.
The Pixel 10 Pro Fold was already a sturdy device. With this year’s version, the company claims to have increased durability by three times. Plus, there is a new glass-ceramic cover and a glass-fiber composite back cover to take up any impact. My Pixel 10 fell a few times from the table and from my pocket, but there wasn’t any visible dent or scratch. Well done, Google.
One drawback of a strong hinge is that you can’t unfold the 11 Pro Fold with one hand, and that’s by design.
The outer display is ever so slightly bigger, but the more observable change is the 3,600-nit display that is an upgrade from last year’s 3,000-nit peak display. This means that you can use the phone in bright conditions better.
Google’s foldable still has a very visible crease in an age where phone makers like Oppo and Honor have managed to reduce the visibility significantly. The crease is more pronounced in bright light, given there is no reflective display on the device.
On the back, there is the new HiLight indicator, which still lights up only for calls from your favourite contacts, and when you are talking with Gemini hands-free. There isn’t much to talk about this feature beyond that.
Software and AI
Reading and watching videos on a foldable is still fun, though a wide foldable might show an edge on videos. The multitasking is good, but you can only open two apps side by side. Some apps that are tuned for foldable are great to use. For instance, Gmail, being a Google app, lets you see your inbox on one side and a particular email on the other. This can help you get through emails faster. However, Slack doesn’t have this split view, and it’s frustrating because we have been through many cycles of Android foldables with apps still not suited for the expanded screen.
Given how quick Apple developer system moves, Android might feel it’s lagging in foldable experiences after the iPhone Duo is out. The camps are divided as to how apps look on Duo’s unfolded phone, but developers are rapidly updating their apps to fit the unfolded screen.
The bubbles, which let you access apps in floating windows and minimize them in a taskbar, are a good idea. That way, you can temporarily look at information in an app without having to make it a full-sized window.
Gemini updates this year were muted. The company built on its idea of Magic Cue to give timely suggestions in different apps. As I mentioned in my Pixel 11 Pro XL review, Rambler was my favorite feature to use in the new Pixel lineups. I could easily reply to emails and texts, and take notes, without involving texting on a wide keyboard.
Camera
Foldables have mostly had inferior cameras to their candybar counterparts for years now. While this year is no different, Google continuing to use the “Pro” moniker for its foldable feels like a disservice. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold cameras are good, but they aren’t Pixel 11 Pro XL good.
There are a few positives with the new version. There is an updated main sensor, still a 48-megapixel one, that lets more light in for photos with better detail. Google has also updated its models to support 30x Super Res Zoom, up from 20x Super Res Zoom.
Even if Google wouldn’t include the same ultrawide and telephoto sensors as the slab Pro devices, I wish they would use the same main sensor on the Fold as the rectangle phone. The telephoto and ultrawide sensors are similar to last year’s device, so there is barely any improvement in images taken from them.
In terms of software features, there is Looks, which can change the tone of an image with different presets, and Magic Capture, which can pick the best frames from a video — useful for when you have pets or kids.
Price
At $1,899, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold is for someone who likes Pixels and wants a foldable, given it’s barely $100 less than the new iPhone Duo and the same price as the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, which are both wide-format phones. In the U.S., the taller Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra starts at $2,099.
In Europe, companies like Xiaomi and Honor are going to release their foldables, too. So Google’s foldable is going to face a lot of competition.

Nonetheless, I have enjoyed using the device because the Pixel 11 Pro Fold’s cameras are competent enough, even if they aren’t a match for the Pixel 11 Pro’s setup, and the screen is nice to use despite the very visible crease.
Design
The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is 5mm thick when unfolded (vs 5.2mm of the Pixel 10 Pro Fold) and 10.1mm thick when folded (vs 10.8 mm of the Pixel 10 Pro Fold). This one is for the spec sheet because you might not feel as much difference. Despite this, the phone is not as thin as a device like the Honor V6 Magic.
The difference you might notice — if you hold both this year’s and last year’s foldables — is that the new device is 19 grams lighter. But if you are buying a new device or switching from another foldable, it’s barely noticeable.
The Pixel 10 Pro Fold was already a sturdy device. With this year’s version, the company claims to have increased durability by three times. Plus, there is a new glass-ceramic cover and a glass-fiber composite back cover to take up any impact. My Pixel 10 fell a few times from the table and from my pocket, but there wasn’t any visible dent or scratch. Well done, Google.
One drawback of a strong hinge is that you can’t unfold the 11 Pro Fold with one hand, and that’s by design.
The outer display is ever so slightly bigger, but the more observable change is the 3,600-nit display that is an upgrade from last year’s 3,000-nit peak display. This means that you can use the phone in bright conditions better.
Google’s foldable still has a very visible crease in an age where phone makers like Oppo and Honor have managed to reduce the visibility significantly. The crease is more pronounced in bright light, given there is no reflective display on the device.
On the back, there is the new HiLight indicator, which still lights up only for calls from your favourite contacts, and when you are talking with Gemini hands-free. There isn’t much to talk about this feature beyond that.
Software and AI
Reading and watching videos on a foldable is still fun, though a wide foldable might show an edge on videos. The multitasking is good, but you can only open two apps side by side. Some apps that are tuned for foldable are great to use. For instance, Gmail, being a Google app, lets you see your inbox on one side and a particular email on the other. This can help you get through emails faster. However, Slack doesn’t have this split view, and it’s frustrating because we have been through many cycles of Android foldables with apps still not suited for the expanded screen.
Given how quick Apple developer system moves, Android might feel it’s lagging in foldable experiences after the iPhone Duo is out. The camps are divided as to how apps look on Duo’s unfolded phone, but developers are rapidly updating their apps to fit the unfolded screen.
The bubbles, which let you access apps in floating windows and minimize them in a taskbar, are a good idea. That way, you can temporarily look at information in an app without having to make it a full-sized window.
Gemini updates this year were muted. The company built on its idea of Magic Cue to give timely suggestions in different apps. As I mentioned in my Pixel 11 Pro XL review, Rambler was my favorite feature to use in the new Pixel lineups. I could easily reply to emails and texts, and take notes, without involving texting on a wide keyboard.
Camera
Foldables have mostly had inferior cameras to their candybar counterparts for years now. While this year is no different, Google continuing to use the “Pro” moniker for its foldable feels like a disservice. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold cameras are good, but they aren’t Pixel 11 Pro XL good.
There are a few positives with the new version. There is an updated main sensor, still a 48-megapixel one, that lets more light in for photos with better detail. Google has also updated its models to support 30x Super Res Zoom, up from 20x Super Res Zoom.
Even if Google wouldn’t include the same ultrawide and telephoto sensors as the slab Pro devices, I wish they would use the same main sensor on the Fold as the rectangle phone. The telephoto and ultrawide sensors are similar to last year’s device, so there is barely any improvement in images taken from them.
In terms of software features, there is Looks, which can change the tone of an image with different presets, and Magic Capture, which can pick the best frames from a video — useful for when you have pets or kids.
Price
At $1,899, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold is for someone who likes Pixels and wants a foldable, given it’s barely $100 less than the new iPhone Duo and the same price as the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, which are both wide-format phones. In the U.S., the taller Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra starts at $2,099.
In Europe, companies like Xiaomi and Honor are going to release their foldables, too. So Google’s foldable is going to face a lot of competition.

title_fa: North Korea linked to massive Binance crypto heist
excerpt_en: The FBI says North Korea was behind the massive $6.3 billion crypto heist that hit Binance on October 29th. The FBI labeled the activity "TraderTraitor" and said that it had observed actors it has connected to hack converting the tokens to Ethereum and preparing for further...
excerpt_fa: The FBI says North Korea was behind the massive $6.3 billion crypto heist that hit Binance on October 29th. The FBI labeled the activity "TraderTraitor" and said that it had observed actors it has connected to hack converting the tokens to Ethereum and preparing for further...
content_en:
The FBI says North Korea was behind the massive $6.3 billion crypto heist that hit Binance on October 29th. The FBI labeled the activity “TraderTraitor” and said that it had observed actors it has connected to hack converting the tokens to Ethereum and preparing for further laundering of the funds. The agency offered few other details or evidence. The statement says:
North Korea linked to massive Binance crypto heist
The FBI says that malicious actors from North Korea stole $6.3 billion worth of Crypto from Binance customers.
The FBI says that malicious actors from North Korea stole $6.3 billion worth of Crypto from Binance customers.
North Korea Responsible for $6 Billion+ Binance Attack
The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026. The FBI refers to this specific North Korean malicious cyber activity as “TraderTraitor.”
The FBI, together with partners at the USSS and IRS-CI, has observed TraderTraitor actors converting stolen assets primarily into Ethereum (ETH). It is expected these assets will then be further laundered by converting them using DeFi and instant swap services as they prepare them for further laundering stages.
As expected, Binance reopened customer withdrawals today after freezing them in the immediate aftermath of the hack.

title_en: Here’s what ‘renoa’ — the first new fiber in 25 years — feels like
title_fa: Here’s what ‘renoa’ — the first new fiber in 25 years — feels like
excerpt_en: Startup Everbloom's new material, renoa, is the first new fiber in 25 years, and it feels very familiar.
excerpt_fa: Startup Everbloom's new material, renoa, is the first new fiber in 25 years, and it feels very familiar.
content_en:
Sometimes it seems like everyone — and every occasion — demands cashmere these days.
Numerous brands sell cashmere sweaters, from Bruno Cucinelli’s $7,900 cable knit cardigan to Quince’s $50 crewneck. Menswear company Loro Piana has made cashmere a cornerstone of its lineup, helping to drive the LVMH division’s valuation above €11 billion. There are even cashmere running shirts.
But as cashmere has spread throughout the fashion industry, it’s not for everyone. It’s still relatively expensive, hard to care for, and environmental fraught. The goats that produce cashmere have been trashing rangelands across Central Asia.
That may change, though. I recently experienced an alternative fiber called renoa, developed by a startup called Everbloom, that’s washable and promises to be more affordable. It could bring the cashmere experience, via a substitute material, to more products and people.
Renoa is made from sources of waste protein, including cashmere and wool scraps as well as down and feather “lint” leftover from the bedding industry. Everbloom processes the waste into a powder and blends it with a biodegradable biopolymer, and the combination is then extruded to the right length and diameter to mimic specific natural fibers.
Renoa was recently approved as the first new fiber classification in 25 years by the U.S. Federal Trade Commission, which regulates fiber labeling in the U.S.
Everbloom has been developing the new fiber for three years, and is currently in the process of scaling up. The startup developed its own AI model for material science, and a cashmere substitute is the first product.
Last month, I stopped by Everbloom’s headquarters in New York City, which sits 15 floors above 5th Avenue, kitty corner from Bryant Park. There, co-founder and CEO Sim Gulati walked me through a range of products made with its company’s cashmere-like renoa, including a crewneck sweater, a pair of knit gloves, and a scarf.
The sweater and gloves were soft and light, but the scarf was the most notable. It didn’t look like much, but it had been through the kind of hell and back that a pure cashmere scarf wouldn’t survive. It was a custom item that Everbloom had knit to test renoa, and Gulati had been wearing and washing it for months, including a trip through the tumble dryer before I saw it. It wasn’t pilled, and Gulati said it hadn’t shrunk, either.
Everbloom is currently working with a range of companies to get renoa into consumer products. The first are likely to feature renoa as a blended fiber, making up around 20% of the material in a cashmere sweater, for example. The first product is expected to hit the market in the second quarter of 2027 Gulati said.
The 80/20 cashmere-renoa blend that I felt was extremely close to the real thing, and Gulati said that additional finishing that accompanies commercial garments should eliminate any differences without compromising the washability and stability of the garment. After my visit, I kept thinking about various items in my closet that could benefit from those features. When renoa lands on shelves next year, I’ll be keeping an eye out for it.

title_en: HomePod Mini 2 first look: Three things I love and one disappointment
title_fa: HomePod Mini 2 first look: Three things I love and one disappointment
excerpt_en: When I first heard about the new $149 HomePod Mini 2 at Apple's Welcome Home event last month, I was disappointed. It's been six years since Apple launched its entry-level smart speaker, and all it got in the second gen was a chip bump, some color glowy stuff, and better...
excerpt_fa: When I first heard about the new $149 HomePod Mini 2 at Apple's Welcome Home event last month, I was disappointed. It's been six years since Apple launched its entry-level smart speaker, and all it got in the second gen was a chip bump, some color glowy stuff, and better...
content_en:
When I first heard about the new $149 HomePod Mini 2 at Apple’s Welcome Home event last month, I was disappointed. It’s been six years since Apple launched its entry-level smart speaker, and all it got in the second gen was a chip bump, some color glowy stuff, and better AirPlay? For $50 more than the original, which launched at $99, Apple didn’t even upgrade the sound system. It felt like the company phoned this one in.
HomePod Mini 2 first look: Three things I love and one disappointment
The new Mini is faster, quieter, and gorgeous in green, but its upgraded Mac speaker feature didn’t work for me.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
Now that I’ve got my hands on a couple and set them up in my home office, I’m more enthused. The Mini 2 is so much faster than the first-gen Mini, playing music in a few seconds and responding to smart home commands just as quickly. If you’re fed up with standing over your HomePod waiting for it to finally do what you asked, then that alone is worth the upgrade.
Here are my three favorite features of the new Mini 2 after spending a couple days with it, and my one big disappointment.
Siri is much snappier and much less chatty
The biggest upgrade for the Mini 2 is Siri AI, but that isn’t available yet. Apple says it’s coming “later” in a software update. However, the basic smart voice assistant has definitely improved. Siri on the Mini 2 is much snappier than on the first-gen Mini, regularly responding in under three seconds. This is thanks to a newer, faster processor (the S10, up from the S5) and Wi-Fi 6E support (up from Wi-Fi 4).
When I asked Siri to play Taylor Swift, a song started in a couple of seconds. It correctly told me who won this year’s World Series in under two seconds, and turned off the light or opened the shades in under three seconds.
That’s a huge improvement over the up to 10 seconds I often have to wait for Siri to get things done on the first-gen Mini. However, asking something harder, like who will win the US midterm elections, still brings up the familiar offer to look at some web results on my iPhone. As I said, Siri AI isn’t here yet.
The other new behavior I am really enjoying is that when I ask Siri to perform a smart home action, such as open the shades or turn on the lights, instead of “OK, Jen,” or “One sec,” followed by a wordy confirmation of the action that I often get on the first-gen Mini, the Mini 2 just does it and doesn’t talk back. It’s not silent for every action, but it’s quiet enough to be a noticeable improvement.
This Mini is gorgeous in green and sounds great
The green color is divine. This is the prettiest small smart speaker I’ve seen — and I’ve tried them all.
Yes, Amazon’s Echo Dot Max’s purple is fun, the Google Home Speaker’s pale green is elegant, but Apple’s deep green is seriously sophisticated. It’s a color that fits in really well in various places around my home, and I’m so glad the company finally released a green option. It’s a big improvement over the slightly garish yellow and orange of the prior-gen Minis and the best of the new colors.
I saw all the colors in person at Apple’s Welcome Home event, and while the pink is pretty, it’s very pale, and the blue is functionally identical to the first-gen blue, maybe a shade lighter. While a lot of folks will be happy with black (don’t get white unless you plan to dust it regularly), the green is my new go-to.
Two green HomePod Mini 2s look so good on the walnut Nanoleaf monitor stand I’m testing; it’s like my office got an instant upgrade. And while Apple didn’t update the speakers in the Mini 2, it’s still a very good speaker for its size, doing a fine job with Bad Bunny’s bass and delivering clear mids and vocals. While $300 is steep for computer speakers, two as a stereo pair in my office definitely delivered on room-filling sound.
You can finally disable touch
A few weeks ago I fumbled for my phone on my nightstand and accidentally hit the top of my HomePod Mini, blaring music in the bedroom at 3AM. My husband was not happy.
A new setting in the Home app now lets you lock the Mini’s top controls. This goes for all HomePods, old and new, and it’s a major quality-of-life upgrade. How often do you intentionally touch the top of your HomePod? I bet far less often than accidentally!
The other new trick for the top of the HomePod is Sound Glow. This makes the LEDs display colors that match the album art of the song you’re playing (it’s also backward compatible with the first-gen Mini and the second-gen HomePod). It’s neat, but only works with Apple Music and Podcasts and is so subtle that I don’t feel it adds much to my music-listening experience.
Signature feature fail
Beyond the speed improvement, the other new feature I was excited about is the HomePod Mini 2’s ability to be the default speaker for your Mac using what Apple calls “a responsive and persistent AirPlay connection.” This creates a wireless point-to-point connection between the computer and the HomePod.
You can pair a single speaker or a stereo pair to your Mac, and the feature also works with the second-gen HomePod. (Two or four HomePod Mini 2s can also now be part of a surround sound setup using the new Apple TV 4K.)
Disappointingly, I couldn’t get the Mac speaker set up to work. I have the required hardware: a Mac that supports Wi-Fi 6E, running the public release of macOS 27.2 (a Mac Mini M4), and HomePods on HomePod Software 27.2. But the Sound pane in my Mac’s settings didn’t offer an option to set a HomePod via AirPlay as the default sound output.
The Mini showed up and connected like any other AirPlay speaker, with the same flaws as regular AirPlay — occasional artifacting, drop-offs, and some lag with notification sounds — along with the Mac defaulting to its built-in speakers when the computer restarts, or anytime I activate Siri on the HomePod. content_en:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the biggest game releases of the year, follow Andrew Webster. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepbackhere.
New Zelda and GTA represent a games industry that no longer exists
The two biggest games of the year launch in November, offering some reprieve from a terrible year.
New Zelda and GTA represent a games industry that no longer exists
The two biggest games of the year launch in November, offering some reprieve from a terrible year.
How it started
The two biggest games of 2026 are set to launch just a few weeks apart in November.
On the one side you have the behemoth that is Grand Theft Auto VI, an experience 13 years in the making, and the sequel to one of the best-selling games in history. Its predecessor, GTA V, has sold a staggering 230 million copies since it launched in 2013, and was re-released across three generations of consoles. Developer Rockstar is a pioneer in the realm of open-world games, dating back to GTA III, and the scale and ambitions of those worlds have steadily grown since then. With GTA V and later Red Dead Redemption 2, the studio’s ideas reached a new level of realism. And the sixth GTA looks poised to eclipse them both, which has created an unprecedented level of demand.
Analyst firm Circana estimates that 29 percent of gamers in the US intend to buy the game, with demand so large it could boost flagging console sales. “Many consumers who have yet to upgrade to a current-generation console may choose to purchase a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series specifically to play the title,” analyst Mat Piscatella says in a statement. GTA VI’s reach is so vast that almost every other major game launched early to avoid it.
The one exception is Nintendo. The company’s tentpole release for the holidays, and its next major exclusive for the Switch 2, is a lavish remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.
The release is notable for a few reasons. For one thing, it’s an attempt from Nintendo to modernize one of the most influential and beloved games in its long history. The original Ocarina of Time was the world’s first introduction to a 3D iteration of Hyrule, which, in turn, made it an early glimpse at what was possible in three-dimensional spaces, laying a blueprint for countless games that came afterward. Nintendo has since expanded on that, turning Switch-era adventures Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom into wide-open adventures designed for player creativity. They went on to become some of the best-selling games for Nintendo’s most successful console.
Ocarina of Time’s launch also comes just ahead of a live-action Zelda movie in 2027, which could catapult the franchise to a new level of prominence. That’s why Nintendo is seemingly the only company unafraid of competing with GTA.
These aren’t just two blockbuster games – they’re two series with the pull to make this a real cultural moment, akin to “Barbenheimer” but for video games. They’re the kind of launches that make it onto Saturday Night Live and have NBA players worried.
It’s just too bad about the rest of the industry.
How it’s going
These major November releases are something of a mirage, two outliers that stand out amid the wreckage that is the rest of the video game industry. While there have been plenty of major releases and great games this year, the main theme of 2026 has been just how dire things have become. Layoffs, studio closures, unpopular business models, the ever-looming threat of AI, and massive increases in hardware costs have combined to create an ominous cloud over the medium.

GTA VI’s reach is so vast that almost every other major game launched early to avoid it.
